### Coimmunoprecipitation (co-IP)

Two 10cm dishes of Min6 cells were lysed with 1ml of co-IP lysis buffer (100mM NaCl, 5mM EDTA, 50mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 1% NP-40, protease inhibitor tablet, phosphatase inhibitor tablet) after being washed once with ice cold PBS. The lysate was rotated at 4°C for 30m, spun at 13,000xg for 20m at 4°C, and the supernatant was collected. 1mg of protein was combined with 10ug of either CMIP antibody (12851-1-AP, Proteintech) or rabbit IgG control antibody (10500C, Thermo Fisher) and rotated overnight at 4°C. The following day, Pierce Protein A/G Magnetic Beads (88802, Thermo Fisher) were warmed to room temperature, washed twice with 1ml TBS-T (150mM NaCl, 50mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 0.05% Tween-20) on a magnet, and resuspended in the original volume of co-IP lysis buffer. 25ul of beads were added to each lysate tube and the solution was rotated at 4°C for 1h. The beads were then washed 3x with 1ml TBS-T, once with 1ml distilled water, and eluted with 30ul of 2X NuPAGE LDS Sample Buffer and 1X NuPAGE Sample Reducing Agent (DTT). The beads were incubated at room temperature for 10m with occasional flicking of the tube, and then the supernatant was extracted on the magnet. The supernatant was incubated at 95°C for 10m and then the samples were run on a gel as detailed in the Western Blot section above. The primary antibodies used for staining were CMIP: (12851-1-AP, Proteintech) and PI3K p85: (#4292, Cell Signaling Technology).

### Immunofluorescence (IF) staining

#### MIN6 NFkB Immunofluorescence

MIN6 cells grown on 384-well CellCarrier Ultra microplates (#6057308, PerkinElmer) were fixed for 10 min in PBS containing 4% PFA (Electron Microscopy Sciences), permeabilized for 15 min in 0.5% Triton X-100 (Sigma-Aldrich), blocked for 1 h in blocking reagent (100 mM Tris HCL pH 8; 150 mM NaCL; 5 g/L Blocking Reagent (#11096176001, Roche)) and treated for 1.5 h with primary antibody diluted in blocking reagent (NF-κB p65/RELA, Rabbit monoclonal antibody, 1:200, #8242, Cell Signaling Technology). Cells were washed three times in PBS and incubated for 0.5 h with fluorescent-labeled secondary antibody in blocking solution (1:500, Alexa Fluor 568 Goat anti-Rabbit IgG, (#A11036, Thermo Fisher Scientific)). Cytoplasmic actin filaments were stained with Phalloidin conjugated with Alexa 647 (1:40, #A22287, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and nuclei were counterstained with Hoechst (1:2000, #H3570, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cells were washed three times in PBS and imaged using the Opera Phenix High Content Screening System (#HH14000000, Perkin Elmer). A minimum of nine fields were acquired per well using 20x water immersion objectives in confocal mode. Image analysis was performed using the Harmony software (PerkinElmer). Cell nuclei were first identified using Hoechst staining and a nuclear region was defined for each cell. Phalloidin staining was then used to detect and define the cytoplasmic region of the cell. RELA fluorescent intensity was measured separately in the nuclear and cytoplasmic regions and a threshold for a nuclear translocation was defined using negative (BSA) and positive (TNF) controls. For each well, the fraction of cells identified for RELA nuclear translocation was calculated.

#### MIN6 LC3B Immunofluorescence

MIN6 cells grown on 384-well CellCarrier Ultra microplates (#6057308, PerkinElmer) were treated for 48 h with 500 μM FFAs or 25 nM of rapamycin (Sigma-Aldrich, R8781) or bafilomycin A1 (Sigma-Aldrich SML1661). Cells were fixed for 20 min in ice-cold methanol (Sigma-Aldrich, 154903), washed twice with PBS, permeabilized for 15 min in 0.5% Triton X-100 (Sigma-Aldrich, 10789704001), washed twice with PBS, blocked for 1 h in 5% BSA in PBS (SeraCare, 1900–0016) and incubated for 1.5 h with primary antibody diluted in blocking reagent (Lc3b (D11) XP® Rabbit mAb, 1:500, #3868, Cell Signaling Technology). Cells were washed four times in PBS and incubated for 45 min with fluorescent-labeled secondary antibody in blocking solution (1:500, Alexa Fluor 568 Donkey anti-Rabbit IgG, (#A10042, Thermo Fisher Scientific)). Nuclei were counterstained with Hoechst (1:2000, #H3570, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cells were washed four times in PBS and imaged using the Opera Phenix High Content Screening System (#HH14000000, Perkin Elmer). A minimum of nine fields were acquired per well using 63x water immersion objectives in confocal mode. Image analysis was performed using the Harmony software (PerkinElmer). Cell nuclei were first identified using Hoechst staining and a nuclear region was defined for each cell. LC3B puncta were then detected based on intensity and size with rapamycin and bafilomycin treatments serving as controls.

#### Primary Human Islet Immunofluorescence

Primary human islets from three independent cadaveric donors were received from the Integrated Islet Distribution Program. Intact islets were dissociated using accutase followed by trituration and stained using Trypan Blue to confirm viability. They were seeded at 15,000/well into 384-well Cell Carrier Ultra microplates (Perkin Elmer, CellCarrier Ultra, #6057300) coated with HTB-9-derived ECM, and treated two days later with FFAs at 250 μM, 500 μM, and 1 mM. After treatment for 5 days, the islets were fixed for 20 min in 3% PFA followed by permeabilization for 20 min with 0.2% TritonX-100. Blocking with 2% BSA in PBS (SeraCare, AP-45100-80) was conducted for 1 h at room temperature, followed by primary incubation with c-peptide antibody (Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank at the University of Iowa, GN-ID4) at 1:100 overnight at 4 °C. The plate was washed 3x with PBS followed by secondary incubation with 568 goat anti-rat (Life technologies, A11077) at 1:1000 and Hoechst (1:2000, #H3570, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 1 h at room temperature. The plate was then washed 5x with PBS and imaged on the Opera Phenix High Content Screening System (#HH14000000, Perkin Elmer). A minimum of nine fields were acquired per well using a 20x water immersion objective in confocal mode. Image analysis was performed using the Harmony software (PerkinElmer). Beta cells were identified and counted by c-peptide positive staining. All three donors displayed similar trends in c2 toxicity; the data presented in Fig. 5C are representative of all donors.

#### iPSC-Derived Beta Cell Immunofluorescence

IPSC-derived beta cells after 28 days of differentiation as per the protocol listed above were dissociated and seeded at 10,000/well into 96-well Cell Carrier Ultra microplates (Perkin Elmer, CellCarrier Ultra, #6055308) coated with HTB-9-derived ECM. These cells were treated three days later with FFAs at 250 μM, 500 μM, and 750 μM for 24, 48, and 72 h followed by fixation with 4% PFA for 30 min at room temperature. The plates were washed twice with PBS, permeabilized for 15 min with 0.5% Triton-X 100, washed twice again with PBS, and blocked with 5% BSA in PBS for 1 h at room temperature. Hoechst was added (1:2000, #H3570, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and incubated for 1 h at room temperature. The plate was then washed thrice with PBS and imaged on the Opera Phenix High Content Screening System (#HH14000000, Perkin Elmer). A minimum of nine fields were acquired per well using a 20x water immersion objective in confocal mode. Image analysis was performed using the Harmony software (PerkinElmer) and the cells were counted.

### ER Calcium Levels

MIN6 cells were plated in 384-well plates (Aurora, Black 384 SQ Well 188 micron Film, #1022–10110) and treated with the FFA library for 24 h prior to readout (n=5 / FFA). Cells were carefully washed three times with HBSS (with calcium, Thermo Fisher Scientific, #14025076) using an automated simultaneous pipettor (analytikjena CyBio® Well vario) and incubated with the fluorescent calcium indicator Fluo4 (2 μM, Life Technologies, #F14202) in DMEM without supplementation for 1 h at room temperature. Then, cells were washed again in HBSS (with calcium) and incubated for another 30 min at room temperature in DMEM without supplementation. Just before the readout, cells were washed in calcium free assay buffer solution (140 mM NaCl, 5 mM KCl, 10 mM HEPES, 2 mM MgCl2, 10 mM EGTA, 10 mM Glucose) and left with 25 μl assay volume per well. Assay plates were immediately transferred to the FLIPR Tetra® High-Throughput Cellular Screening System. The plate was recorded with a frequency of 1Hz for 10 min. Baseline was recorded for 30 s before the automated liquid transfer system of the FLIPR added the SERCA inhibitor Thapsigargin (final concentration 10 μM) in calcium free assay buffer. The resulting passive efflux of calcium from the ER induced a transient cytosolic fluorescence signal and the peak amplitudes were used to indirectly quantify ER calcium levels (See Fig. S3A). The resulting trajectories were corrected for a pipetting artifact and baseline normalized. Log2 Fold changes were calculated according to plate location specific negative (BSA) controls. We allowed for the exclusion of one outlier / FFA / plate (n=5) based on a 3-sigma cutoff. P-values were calculated with Student’s t-test (two-sided) and corrected for multiple testing (Benjamini & Hochberg).

### Glucose Stimulated Insulin Secretion (GSIS)

To measure GSIS, cells were plated in 96-well plates (Perkin Elmer, CellCarrier Ultra, #6055308) and treated with the FFA library for 24 h prior to readout (n=6 / FFA). First, cells were pre-incubated in Krebs Ringer Buffer (KRB) with 2.8 mM glucose for 1 h and then stimulated with fresh KRB containing 16.7 mM glucose for another hour. The supernatant was then transferred to a mouse insulin ELISA (Thermo Fisher, EMINS) at a dilution of 1:150. The cells were imaged on the Opera Phenix High Content Screening System, (#HH14000000, Perkin Elmer) and subsequently counted via Hoechst nuclear staining using Harmony software (PerkinElmer). A minimum of four fields were acquired per well using a 10x air objective in a confocal mode. The insulin concentrations measured via ELISA were normalized to the number of cells in each respective well.

### Membrane Fluidity Assay

This assay has been well established and optimized in INS-1E cells, a rat beta cell line. INS-1E cells were seeded at 20,000 cells per well in a CellCarrier Ultra 96-well plate (Perkin Elmer). Cells were incubated for 24 h, washed once with PBS, treated with BSA-bound fatty acids in a serum-free media and further incubated for 18 h at 37°C. Cells were washed twice with PBS and stained with Laurdan dye (6-dodecanoyl-2-dimethylaminoaphthalene) (Thermofisher) at 10 μM for 45 min. Cells were washed twice with PBS and images were acquired using an Opera Phenix High-Content Screening system (Perkin Elmer). Temperature (37°C) and carbon dioxide (5%) were controlled during live-cell imaging. Cells were excited with a 405 nm laser and the emission recorded between 435 and 480 nm (ordered phase) and between 500 and 550 nm (disordered phase). Images were analyzed using Harmony High-Content Imaging and Analysis Software (Perkin Elmer) and data represented as general polarization (GP) index as calculated by GP = (intensityorder - intensitydisorder)/(intensityorder + intensitydisorder) (Harris, Best, and Bell 2002; Parasassi et al. 1991).

# Using Generative Artificial Intelligence When Writing Letters of Recommendation

**Authors:** Juliana Coraor Fried; Natasha R. Johnson; Andrea Pelletier; Adam Landman; Deborah Bartz

**Affiliations:** Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts; | Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts; | Department of Emergency Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, and vice president and chief information and digital officer, Mass General Brigham, Somerville, Massachusetts;

## Abstract

Artificial intelligence (AI) provides an opportunity to streamline tasks within academic medicine. Generative AI (genAI) models, specifically, have the capacity to generate new written content, follow detailed instructions for product improvement, and incorporate content from supplemental data sources. While a part of the professional responsibility of faculty in academic medicine, writing letters of recommendation (LORs) is often time consuming and repetitive candidate to candidate. Yet, crafting these letters well is paramount to convey an applicant’s unique attributes in a time when pass/fail grading and remote interviews are increasingly common.

In this article, the authors provide an approachable framework for the ethical use of genAI to assist with writing LORs in academic medicine. They briefly discuss the fundamental structure of genAI, the advantages between several genAI models specifically for the task of letter writing, privacy concerns that can develop when using genAI, iterative methods to develop effective prompts to craft letter drafts, personalization of finalized content, genAI use to identify bias, and appropriate documentation of AI usage.

Once practiced, this process can prevent the need for shortcuts, such as copying and pasting from CVs or re-using previously written letters between candidates, that currently sacrifice letter quality to reduce writing time. Ethical use, privacy, and disclosure necessitate a deliberate framework for the use of genAI in letter writing. Future research is needed to inform the development of a specific AI model to generate LORs. The framework presented here provides faculty with the steps needed to begin incorporating genAI into their letter writing practice.

Since initial conceptions of artificial intelligence (AI), skeptics have postulated AI would perpetually be limited in its ability to rival the creativity and complexity of the human mind.1 Today, the AI frontier has advanced far beyond these expectations.2,3 Within the academic medicine and scientific professions, people have used generative AI (genAI) to write clinical medical records,4 craft personal statements,5 evaluate learners,6,7 revise primary research articles,8 and collate and summarize literature findings.8 GenAI is particularly helpful to humans in completing tasks that generate new content while following instructions and incorporating facts from supplemental data sources.3

A career in academic medicine requires faculty to collaborate with, advocate for, and promote trainees and colleagues during their professional growth. As such, we are often called to write letters of recommendation (LORs) to support our trainees’ and colleagues’ applications to formal training programs, award or grant candidacy, and academic promotion. At a time when standardized tests and professional education programs are moving to pass/fail grading and many interviews are now remote encounters,9 the stalwart LOR remains one of the few robust, holistic metrics for in-depth insight into the character and quality of the applicant.10

However, the LOR faces several challenges, key among them the inordinately time-consuming nature of crafting a high-quality, candidate-specific letter.11 Likely our ideals for ourselves as letter writers are often not realized; we are often shoehorning this task into our otherwise stuffed schedules of competing demands. Thus, we may take shortcuts, using previously written LORs as templates to be modified from one candidate to the next, cutting and pasting from the documents provided by the candidate, and writing and submitting quickly to meet deadlines.11 When not crafted exceedingly well, LORs can perpetuate harm, particularly to disadvantaged groups.10 Multiple studies have shown that there is pervasive racial and gender bias specifically in LORs in academic medicine.10,12,13 Interventions to date to correct this bias have been insufficient to solve the problem.14,15

GenAI, when utilized well, has the potential to improve the writing experience for mentors and simultaneously developing stronger letters unique to each candidate while minimizing bias. In a small study comparing letters of support for promotion, human reviewers were unable to distinguish between human- versus AI-authored letters.16 As medical education leaders and scientific mentors, each of us on this authorship team writes many LORs each year, often all within the same month during specific application seasons. Here, we outline our framework for utilizing genAI to write our LORs, informed initially by literature developed in the informatics and business sectors and refined for medical trainees through our own practical experience using this technology over the last year. Our structured framework described below has allowed our team to reduce our writing steps and time while maintaining our style, tone, and desired level of candidate recommendation.

While the academic medicine and scientific communities have discussed guidelines for the ethical use of genAI in research methodologies and scientific writing,17,18 we as a profession have yet to critically examine how AI might best be used and disclosed in the LOR writing process. Though not yet formally studied, we provide our method to inform today’s safe use of genAI to write LORs in academic medicine, addressing technical functionalities, an iterative improvement process, and the unique challenges that can arise.

## Choosing a GenAI Model

GenAI is a form of AI that creates new content. For example, large language models (LLMs) are a type of genAI that specializes in text generation; these models are trained on vast data sets to predict the next word or sentence in a text sequence.19 Popular LLMs such as ChatGPT 3.5 (OpenAI), Gemini (Google), and Claude (Anthropic) are general-purpose models that excel at generating text and have easy to use chat interfaces that allow the user to interact conversationally with the platform.19,20 Meta’s LLaMA (Large Language Model Meta AI) also excels at text generation but is distinct due to its efficiency, lower resource requirements, and non-commercial license.21 LLMs can also be integrated into other software. For instance, Microsoft 365 Copilot combines OpenAI’s GPT models with Microsoft Office applications, allowing users to generate drafts or assist with revisions directly in Word.22

All these LLMs are suitable for drafting and revising LORs. Given the AI-generated LOR privacy concerns we address in the next section, the choice of which model to use may already be made for a faculty member if their institution has developed and encourages the use of enterprise-grade information security protections within a specific LLM product.

## Addressing Privacy Concerns

Since its creation, genAI has come under scrutiny for privacy concerns.23 Researchers have discovered that personally identifiable data have been distributed in genAI training data sets.24 Interaction data and user prompts are often saved locally and can be accessed in the event of a cyberbreach.24 Even without malicious intent, genAI models have been known to store and regurgitate personal information when prompted, raising concern that any data used in a genAI setting fundamentally can no longer be considered private.25 While countries have begun instituting protections to address these flaws and meet data security and consumer privacy expectations, privacy when using such technology is not guaranteed.26

We strongly recommend that individuals work with their institution to review policies, guidance, and tools for using LLMs for personally identifiable information. Some institutions have created specialized LLM environments or “sandboxes” that enable employees to access LLMs in a secure environment.27 Using these environments, faculty will be able to create LORs that include personal information without concern for sharing the data with the LLMs or vendors. If an institution lacks a secure environment, faculty should consult institutional leadership to explore safe LLM options. Faculty also can consider using secure health care-focused LLMs like Doximity’s GPT28 but should still review privacy and data sharing terms closely. They should avoid using public LLMs without strict data-sharing restrictions, as even de-identified sensitive content may carry re-identification risks.29

## Choosing an Approach

Writing in any form is best done iteratively, and this is particularly important when writing with AI.30 GenAI should be seen as an assistant to the writer, but it cannot and should not replace the human component. An effective LOR writer needs to convey both the relationship they have with the applicant and the personal, humanizing aspects of that person.31 The question is how to best intermingle the human and AI contributions. In our experience, there are 2 main approaches that we have termed AI-as-editor and AI-as-author.

In the AI-as-editor approach, we write the letter ourselves in the traditional manner, adding aspects of the applicant’s resume and personal anecdotes about their performance. We then ask the AI to revise the letter with very specific instructions on what aspect(s) needs improvement. For example, we can ask the AI to elevate the central tone to impart the relationship with the applicant or to highlight certain themes and strengths. The primary benefit of the AI-as-editor option is that it is closer to the classic method of writing LORs and is akin to sending the letter to another collaborator for revision. We think this method would be best suited to individuals who have an established protocol for writing LORs and are hoping to incorporate AI for a specific task, such as to minimize bias or improve the clarity, standardization, and impact of their letters.

The AI-as-author approach, which may appear complicated at first, has the potential to dramatically increase efficiency and improve standardization for those who write many letters. In this process, we use a series of prompts to focus the text that AI produces in different portions of the letter in an iterative manner, integrating the human component throughout and improving cohesion of the piece.30

Both AI-as-editor and AI-as-author have benefits, which we use to decide which approach is best depending on our relationship with the applicant. For example, for candidates we know well, we typically use the AI-as-editor approach, creating a human-derived first draft focusing on our many specific personal experiences with and feedback on the candidate. Meanwhile, we find the AI-as-author approach to work well for candidates we do not know well personally, such as when serving as outside “at arm’s length” reviewers for colleagues up for academic promotion for whom we are objectively reviewing a resume only, without the luxury of a professional relationship with the candidate.

## The Process of Prompt Engineering

While genAI can create sophisticated content, its ability to generate material that is fully aligned with the desire of the user is largely determined by the human prompt or the input to the LLM. Prompts can be deconstructed into 4 fundamental components: instruction, context, the input data, and the output indicator.32 Instruction describes the specific task one desires the model to perform. Context provides external information about why and to what purpose this prompt is being submitted and can be important for improving applicability to the scenario at hand. Input data represents the scenario for which the user wishes to receive an answer, and the output indicator is simply the format of the desired final output.32

Prompt engineering is the practice of iteratively designing the input to LLMs to elicit desired and accurate responses.33,34 For example, consider the task of writing a LOR for an associate professor at another institution who is applying for tenure at her school. Our prompt in this situation could be: I am an Associate Professor of [specialty] at [school name] with [x] years of experience in [field] and have worked with [applicant name] for the past [y] years as a collaborator on [project]. Write a letter of recommendation for [applicant name] to support her promotion from Assistant Professor to Associate Professor that should convey she is a national expert in [specific field]. The instruction is inherent in “write a letter of recommendation” and provides the output indicator (LOR). The context for this prompt is the first sentence naming the relationship between the writer and the applicant. Other content we may provide includes specific information, such as the promotion criteria at the candidate’s home institution or the candidate’s CV. The input data can be found in the latter half of the second sentence in which we convey the specific scenario under scrutiny, namely the promotion from assistant professor to associate professor. We display an example of LOR prompt engineering using these 4 components in Figure 1.

## Developing the Letter

We start by opening a new interface chat session to ensure the model does not accidently insert any erroneous information from any previous genAI tasks. To begin, we recommend breaking the letter-writing process into several smaller subtasks.33 Such subtasks include constructing the LOR structure (as exemplified in the prompt engineering section above), crafting the letter’s message, outlining the key points, adding details, quantifying skill, and modifying the tone. Example prompts to complete these tasks for writing a LOR for faculty promotion can be found in Figure 1. This will generate the first iteration of the letter.

Instructions should guide the genAI model to focus the letter on a particular message,34 which we refine or highlight in next drafts. The prompt should stress a particular angle that should be emphasized about the quality of the candidate, such as their clinical or research prowess, empathetic or decisive manner, or extensive work experience in the field. Being detailed and transparent regarding the intended message will ensure this specific, desired messaging will be featured prominently throughout the suggested text and will make the letter more impactful.34 We can combine this step with instructions that detail a desired outline of the letter structure by guiding the model to focus on specific aspects of the candidate’s resume and experience that would appeal to the letter reader. For example, for a medical student applying to residency, we can instruct the model to “include a paragraph dedicated to their clinical experience and talents, a second paragraph dedicated to their research, and a third paragraph dedicated to their prior work in education.” We can prompt the genAI model “to emphasize throughout the letter their team-building and problem-solving attributes” or “incorporate throughout the letter their interest in mentorship of women and underrepresented minority colleagues.”

We then add details from the applicant’s CV or other documents to flesh out the LOR specifically for this candidate. To do so, we manually create a list of key accomplishments from their CV or copy and paste relevant content from their CV into the LLM. Some LLM interfaces, such as Microsoft Office 365 Copilot, have an option for uploading documents.

Lastly, we tailor the letter to suit our chosen level of recommendation.31,35 Perhaps the most important instruction to provide upfront is to include a statement regarding the quality of the candidate in the letter, which may describe how this candidate compares to others we have worked with.36 Language such as “top 10%,” “top 1%,” “one of the top 5 students in my class,” or “the best researcher I have ever worked with” are much more useful than superlatives such as “excellent,” “great,” or “good” that can have different meanings for different writers and different readers.36 We often include in quotes specific descriptions of how our home institution views this candidate (e.g., “will be actively recruiting this applicant,” “are excited to see their career grow,” or “will be a welcome addition to any program”). If specific language, such as percentiles, is desired, we explicitly tell the model to include it.

Once we have organized our materials and prompts for the model, the development of the initial draft takes just a few seconds. However, this truly is a process of iterative refinement, and we never use a first draft as the final draft. The most common stumbling block we find in this letter development process is that the text the genAI produces is close to what we want to convey but not quite exact. We then further refine the letter either with the human-as-editor approach to edit to the exact language and message we want, or we can be very specific with the next genAI text prompt, inserting the prior text and telling it with as much specificity as possible how the text should be changed in the next draft. This latter method may need to be repeated several times.

## Crafting Tone and Personalizing the Letter

The more detailed the context we provide to the genAI model, the more relevant and helpful the final product will be.34 This extends to providing information about us as the author, such as how long we have known the applicant and from what perspective we will be attesting to their potential.36

We can create the tone we desire through several strategies.37 One is to directly guide the model to craft the content in a certain voice (e.g., more “formal,” “conversational,” “sophisticated”). GenAI can go so far as to write the letter in the voice of a specific person or professional role.37 We have used this function by asking the program to draft the letter as if it was written “by the CEO of a pharmaceutical company” for an applicant to a science leadership position or “by a U.S. Senator” for a veteran student applying into a military residency. Similarly, once a first draft of the letter is created (either by the author or by AI), in the next prompt, we state what is wrong with the current tone and content of the letter and give the program specific instructions on how to fix it. This allows the model to iterate on the content.30 Another option for specifying tone is to provide the model with previous writing samples in the desired voice, which would be our previous human-derived letters.37

The last step in customizing this letter requires us to incorporate personal anecdotes or feedback quotations about the candidate.36 These stories and quotations often are the key to composing a memorable LOR and provide priceless insight into the core components of the candidate’s qualities that cannot be conveyed by academic accomplishments alone. Furthermore, including these features highlights our relationship to the applicant and strengthens our unique authority to testify to their talents. This step is likely heavily or solely human-derived regardless of our chosen approach thus far (AI-as-author or AI-as-editor).

## Minimizing Bias

It has been well established that LORs remain fraught with racial and gender bias. Human-derived LORs for women and racial minority applicants are more likely to emphasize their effort and personal characteristics rather than their accomplishments.10,38,39

Using genAI affords us an opportunity to correct this bias by improving standardization across letters and bringing awareness to any differences in applicant descriptors between letters. In a single-masked quasi-experimental study where academic physicians reviewed LORs written by either humans or AI, human-authored letters contained significantly more female-associated words, while the majority of AI-authored letters used more male-associated words.16

Even for faculty who feel strongly about writing their own LOR from salutation to signature, we recommend they ask genAI as a final step to deliberately probe their letter for potential bias. For example, we ask genAI the following questions: “How many agentic adjectives appear in this LOR?” “How many communal adjectives appear?” “How many publications are mentioned in this letter?” and “Does this letter emphasize accomplishments or effort more?” While current genAI models still struggle to identify some of these particular features, using them in combination with other resources, such as agentic language databases, shows significant promise.40 Once unintentional bias is identified, we rebalance the text to fix it.

Although a promising resource, genAI itself can be biased towards or against certain groups simply due to it being trained using human-derived data, thus amplifying any human-derived bias in those data.41 OpenAI has tackled this from the user end, harnessing humans to provide feedback on ChatGPT responses and then using that feedback to retrain their model, a technique that is still prone to bias by virtue of the continued use of humans in the retraining process.42 Google has been accused of introducing counter bias in its efforts to retrain Gemini on the front end, generating controversy over its racially inaccurate portrayals of historically prominent figures and highly one-sided perspectives on political topics.43 However, one of the benefits of using AI in letter writing is that the gender, race, and other identifiers of the applicant can be masked to the program, helping to reduce some of the bias inherent in a human author.

## Documenting Usage

While many are still in the process of drafting precise guidelines for how to disclose the use of genAI in writing, most institutions agree that some sort of disclosure should occur.44,45 As the role of genAI in writing will likely expand, we agree that it is important to set documentation standards early. Before we started using AI to assist in writing LORs, we investigated our institution’s own policy, and we watch for changes at our institution regarding AI use and disclosure.46

Next, when we are approached to write a LOR, we vary our disclosure to the letter requestor depending on the position of the person making the request. If the candidate themself asks for a letter, part of our initial conversation with them is to discuss the strength of the letter we can write for them and the documents we need to assist in the letter writing. During this conversation, we also inform the candidate that we currently use genAI to assist in all our writing to streamline the process, correct grammar, and mitigate bias but that we guarantee the content and assertions will be ours alone and will appropriately express our recommendation of them as a candidate. If we are asked to write a LOR from a third party, such as a department chair for an arms-length letter for academic promotion, we do not disclose our planned use of AI when we agree to write the letter; instead we include the disclosure (see below) in the letter itself. This is our personal practice. We could find no guidance from experts in ethical writing or published guidelines in the current literature to inform our practice.

We advise everyone to include their use of genAI in the LORs themselves in preparation for more stringent disclosure guidelines and for normalization of the use of genAI, both of which we believe are likely ahead. We accomplish this disclosure in a final, short paragraph at the end of the letter. With the concern that acknowledging this usage may potentially bias evaluators against these letters,47 we do this in a way that normalizes our use of AI to avoid any one letter being “flagged” as inauthentic. Lastly, we use this documentation to make it clear that we, the human signing the letter, ultimately take full responsibility for the content.

An example of our disclosure is: I use AI to assist in writing all my letters of recommendation and do so because I believe it creates a better reflection of my thoughts on each applicant. Portions of this letter were written in conjunction with the assistance of [AI program] to ensure consistency of letter tone and content specific to [applicant name] and for minimization of unconscious bias. All AI-generated portions have been reviewed and checked for accuracy by me as the undersigned.

## Reviewing the Final Product

GenAI, while highly promising, must be used with an awareness of its limitations and potential harms. These programs have shown a concerning inability to discern fact from fiction, repeating inaccurate information from the internet or even creating fictional content.48,49 Therefore, it is essential that human authors review all content and confirm the validity and unbiased nature of any AI produced text. As with any writing, we highly recommend a last step to scrutinize the final product for such errors. It is in this final editing phase where we add in identifying information, such as applicant name, institutional names, and other sensitive information if we deliberately kept it from the model given the above privacy concerns.

## Current Limitations and Future Opportunities

The recommendations we provide here are primarily based on our experience and the informatics and business literature. There is a significant need for rigorous, quantitative research to determine the most effective strategies for using LLMs in drafting LORs for a wide variety of candidates and application types. Specifically, comparative studies are required to evaluate the performance and cost-effectiveness of various LLMs in the context of LOR generation. Further research should also focus on optimizing prompt engineering to maximize the quality and relevance of generated content.

As the field matures, there is potential to develop a specialized, user-friendly AI assistant for LORs that systematically guides users through inputting candidate information and evaluations and utilizes optimized prompts to generate high-quality recommendations. Research into the costs and the cost savings in training people on these AI-assistants will also be needed.

We do recognize that people hold varying degrees of eagerness to adopt a new technology, and several sociotechnical factors across individual, technical, organizational, and regulator domains may influence a person’s willingness to use AI for writing letters of recommendation.50 For example, some individuals may lack trust in the accuracy or appropriateness of AI-generated content, while others may avoid AI due to unfamiliarity or perceived technical complexity. Additional investigation is needed to fully understand and address these barriers.

## Conclusion

GenAI has the potential to maximize benefits to both letter writers and applicants, creating a win-win scenario by automating administrative tasks while also reducing unconscious bias and elevating the impact of a letter’s message. There are suitable approaches for all individuals regardless of technological prowess. For beginners, genAI can be a great tool to revise already written letters and, for the most advanced, it can be a transformative technique for streamlining the whole letter writing process. Furthermore, by standardizing our approach to identifying and correcting unconscious bias in letter writing, genAI boosts our ability to create a fair application process. We encourage all in academic medicine to explore the potentials of AI in their own letter writing, and we are excited to see how this may benefit the promotion of our trainees and faculty colleagues alike.

# Replica-nondiagonal solutions in the SYK model

**Authors:** Irina Aref’eva Email: arefeva@mi-ras.ru Mikhail Khramtsov Email: khramtsov@mi-ras.ru Maria Tikhanovskaya and Email: tikhanovskaya@mi-ras.ru Igor Volovich Affiliation: Steklov Mathematical Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences, Gubkina str. 8, 119991, Moscow, Russia Email: volovich@mi-ras.ru

## Abstract

We study the SYK model in the large $N$ limit beyond the replica-diagonal approximation. First we show that there are exact replica-nondiagonal solutions of the saddle point equations for $q=2$ for any finite replica number $M$ . In the interacting $q=4$ case we are able to construct the numerical solutions, which are in one-to-one correspondence to the analytic solutions of the quadratic model. These solutions are singular in the $M\to 0$ limit in both quadratic and quartic interaction cases. The calculations of the on-shell action at finite integer $M$ show that the nondiagonal replica-symmetric saddles are subleading in both quadratic and quartic cases.

We also study replica-nondiagonal solutions of the SYK in the strong coupling limit. For arbitrary $q$ we show that besides the usual solutions of the replica-diagonal saddle point equations in the conformal limit, there are also replica-nondiagonal solutions for any value of $M$ (including zero). The specific configurations that we study, have factorized time and replica dependencies. The corresponding saddle point equations are separable at strong coupling, and can be solved using the Parisi ansatz from spin glass theory. We construct the solutions which correspond to the replica-symmetric case and to one-step replica symmetry breaking. We compute the regularizized free energy on these solutions in the limit of zero replicas. It is observed that there are nondiagonal solutions with the regularized free energy lower than that of the standard diagonal conformal solution.

## 1 Introduction

The Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model [1, 2, 3, 4] is a quantum mechanical model of $N$ Majorana fermions with disordered interactions that is solvable at large $N$ in the strong coupling limit. It was proposed [2] as a solvable toy model for holographic description of quantum gravity in the AdS2 spacetime (see [5] for a review). This idea is justified by the fact that the SYK model displays emergent approximate conformal symmetry in the strong coupling regime [2, 3, 6] and that it exhibits maximal quantum chaos [2, 3, 7] at strong coupling. The Goldstone mode corresponding to the conformal symmetry is connected to the gravitational mode in the effective description of the Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity in the AdS2 bulk [3, 9, 4, 11, 8, 10]. Its dynamics in the leading order in inverse coupling turned out to be completely solvable [10, 12, 14, 13], and in the leading order in $1/N$ all correlation functions of operators dual to the matter fields in the bulk were computed as well [15]. While the precise bulk dual theory is still unknown, the SYK model has already allowed to obtain significant insight in the physics of black holes and wormholes [17, 18].

The defining characteristic of the SYK model is the quenched disorder which randomizes the couplings between sites. Under the assumption that the system is self-averaging, one can perform averaging over the disorder by introducing replicas, and obtain the path integral in terms of auxiliary fields $G_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})$ and $\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})$ , where $\alpha,\beta$ are the replica indices [2, 4, 12]. The results for SYK regarding the large $N$ solution and thermodynamics, are obtained under the assumption that the auxiliary fields are diagonal in replicas. This assumption is justified by the exact diagonalization numerics [3, 12, 19, 17], and by a physical qualitative argument11 1 We discuss this argument and its applicability in detail in Appendix C. [20, 21, 7] that prohibits realization of replica-nondiagonal behavior. Besides that, the work which studied spin glass phases (which are usually realized as particular replica-nondiagonal saddle points of the free energy path integral) [1, 20, 21, 23, 24, 22] found no numerical evidence of glassy behavior in the fermionic SYK model and provided several analytic arguments of why there should not be spin glass physics. However, all these considerations do not conclusively exclude the existence of general replica-nondiagonal saddle points of the path integral at either finite or zero replicas (in the case of the free energy). Meanwhile, recent work [17, 26, 25] hints that replica-nondiagonal saddle points in annealed quantities, such as the spectral form factor, are responsible for manifestations of quantum chaotic behavior in black holes and possible recovery of information from the black hole, which is lost at the semiclassical level, via holographic duality.

Motivated by these points, in the present work we study the replica-nondiagonal large $N$ saddle points of of the SYK model at general replica number. We start off with the $q=2$ variant of the model (where $q$ is the degree of the interacting Hamiltonian). We obtain a family of analytic replica-nondiagonal solutions of the saddle point equations of the disorder-averaged partition function for $M$ replicas of the SYK chain, where $M$ can be understood as an arbitrary real non-negative number. These solutions have an important property of being singular at $M\to 0$ . This means that these saddles do not contribute to the free energy. Computing the on-shell action on these solutions at finite replica number, we show that for analytically continued $0<M<1$ there is a nontrivial phase structure of the path integral, however for $M>1$ the standard diagonal solution always dominates. As a next step, we use these analytic solutions in the $q=2$ model to construct nondiagonal numerical solutions to the exact saddle point equations in the interacting $q=4$ variant of the model. These numerical solutions also exhibit the singular behavior at $M\to 0$ and $J=0$ . In the $q=4$ case the replica-nondiagonal saddles are also subleading in the replica partition function at $M>1$ .

In the second part of the work, we focus on the strong coupling, or IR limit of the SYK model. In this limit one can find analytic replica-nondaigonal solutions in the interacting model either at finite replica number or in the limit of zero replicas. We study the class of solutions, for which the time dependence and replica dependence are factorized. In this case the saddle point equations separate in the strong coupling limit. The solution is then constructed by solving the equation for the temporal part in the same way as in the replica-diagonal case, and by solving an algebraic equation for the replica part. We perform the latter by using the Parisi ansatz [27, 28]. The algebraic equation for the replica dependence in the zero replica limit transforms into an integral equation. To solve it, we restrict ourselves to the step-function ansatz, which corresponds to the one-step replica symmetry breaking. We study the solutions at $M=0$ and compute the regularized free energy on the corresponding saddle points.

The paper is organized as follows. In the section 2 we briefly review the main features of the replica-diagonal saddle-point of SYK, and discuss the non-perturbativity of the exact replica-nondiagonal saddles. We start the study of the replica-nondiagonal solutions in the section 3, which is devoted to the quadratic variation of the model. The exact nondiagonal solutions and their properties are discussed. The next section 4 contains a description and the results of the numerical study of exact saddles in the interacting $q=4$ model, and also a general remark on the large replica number limit. In the section 5 we switch gears to the study of replica-nondiagonal solutions in the strong coupling limit. Assuming the factorized ansatz, we derive the reduced saddle point equations and explain in detail the general strategy for constructing the solutions and computing the regularized free energy in the zero replicas limit. Subsequently, in the section 6 we construct the solutions in the one-step replica symmetry breaking ansatz and compute the leading contribution to the regularized free energy in the strong coupling limit. In the next section 7 we make some comments about generating other solutions using the reparametrization symmetry, possible holographic interpretation in particular cases and about solutions beyond the strong coupling limit. We discuss our results and unanswered questions in the section 8. The appendix A provides a brief introduction to Parisi matrices and derivations of a few formulas used in the main text, and the appendix B contains a few general formulae regarding the computation of on-shell action in different cases. In the appendix C we present some general considerations of the disordered correlation functions and other observables and their relation to our results.

## 2 Setup

The object of our study is the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model [2, 3, 4], which is a theory of $N\gg 1$ interacting Majorana fermions in $0+1$ dimensions22 2 In this paper we work in the Euclidean time, unless mentioned otherwise.. The Hamiltonian is given by

$$ H=\frac{i^{q/2}}{q!}\sum_{i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{q}=1}^{N}j_{i_{1}i_{2}\dots i_{q}}\psi_{i_{1}}\psi_{i_{2}}\dots\psi_{i_{q}}\,. $$

Here $\psi_{i}$ are the Majorana fermions, and $j_{i_{1}\dots i_{q}}$ are totally antisymmetric couplings randomized via the Gaussian distribution:

$$ P(j_{i_{1}\dots i_{q}})=\sqrt{\frac{N^{q-1}}{2(q-1)!\pi J^{2}}}\ \mathrm{e}^{-\frac{N^{q-1}j_{i_{1}\dots i_{q}}^{2}}{2(q-1)!J^{2}}}\,. $$

To calculate a physical quantity in this model, one has to average over the disorder using the rules which follow from the distribution (2):

$$ \overline{j_{i_{1}\dots i_{q}}}=0\,,\qquad\overline{j_{i_{1}\dots i_{q}}j_{i_{1}\dots i_{q}}}=\frac{(q-1)!J^{2}}{N^{q-1}}\quad\text{(no sum)}\,. $$

To study physically meaningful quantities, one usually has to average over all realizations of the disorder. The free energy of the model with quenched disorder is given by

$$ F=-\frac{1}{\beta}\overline{\log Z}\,, $$

where $Z=\text{Tr}\ \mathrm{e}^{-\beta H}$ . To simplify evaluating the disorder average, one employs the replica trick, which we write in the form [29]:

$$ \overline{\ln Z}=\lim_{M\to 0}\frac{\ln\overline{Z^{M}}}{M}\,. $$

In the case of integer $M$ on the right hand side there is a path integral over $M$ copies of SYK, so the fields now carry an additional index $\alpha=1,\dots,M$ . We study the case of integer values of $M$ separately. The limit $M\to 0$ requires an analytic continuation, which will be considered on a particular ansatz.

One can calculate the disorder average for the replica partition function and rewrite it in terms of the path integral over $O(N)$ -invariant auxiliary fields with replica indices. The derivation was presented in detail in [12, 4]. After this procedure, one obtains the following expression for the replica partition function:

$$ \displaystyle\overline{Z(\beta)^{M}}=\int DGD\Sigma\ \text{Pf}[\delta_{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\tau}-\hat{\Sigma}_{\alpha\beta}]^{N}\times \displaystyle\exp\left[-\frac{N}{2}\int_{0}^{\beta}\int_{0}^{\beta}d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2}\left(\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})G_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})-\frac{J^{2}}{q}G_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})^{q}\right)\right]\,, $$

where $G$ is the bilocal field which has the meaning of the Majorana fermion two-point function, and $\Sigma$ is the auxiliary bilocal field33 3 Here and henceforth the hat denotes the integral operator corresponding to the kernel given by the bilocal field. which has the meaning of the fermion self-energy. These bilocal fields are supposed to satisfy the antisymmetry condition

$$ G_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})=-G_{\beta\alpha}(\tau_{2},\tau_{1})\,;\qquad\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})=-\Sigma_{\beta\alpha}(\tau_{2},\tau_{1})\,. $$

In the present work we essentially study the saddle points of (6) for different values of $M$ . The saddle points of the path integral are defined by the following equations:

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\tau}G_{\alpha\gamma}(\tau,\tau^{\prime\prime})-\int d\tau^{\prime}G_{\alpha\beta}(\tau,\tau^{\prime})\Sigma_{\beta\gamma}(\tau^{\prime},\tau^{\prime\prime}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\delta_{\alpha\gamma}\delta(\tau-\tau^{\prime\prime})\,; \displaystyle\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}(\tau,\tau^{\prime}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle J^{2}G_{\alpha\beta}(\tau,\tau^{\prime})^{q-1}\,. $$

### 2.1 Review of the replica-diagonal solution

The replica partition function (6) has a family of replica-diagonal saddle points, which have been extensively studied in the literature [2, 3, 4, 7, 12, 15]. One assumes the ansatz

$$ G_{\alpha\beta}(\tau,\tau^{\prime})=G(\tau,\tau^{\prime})\delta_{\alpha\beta}\,;\qquad\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}(\tau,\tau^{\prime})=\Sigma(\tau,\tau^{\prime})\delta_{\alpha\beta}\,. $$

The quenched average in this case coincides with the annealed average up to subleading orders in $1/N$ expansion [4, 16]:

$$ \underbrace{\overline{\log Z_{\text{RD}}}}_{\text{quenched}}=\underbrace{\log\overline{Z_{\text{RD}}}}_{\text{annealed}}+O\left(\frac{1}{N^{q-2}}\right)\,, $$

which means that up to subleading orders in $1/N$ one can take off the replica indices in the path integral (6):

$$ \overline{Z_{\text{RD}}}=\int DGD\Sigma\ \text{Pf}[\partial_{\tau}-\hat{\Sigma}]^{N}\exp\left[-\frac{N}{2}\int_{0}^{\beta}\!\!\!\!\int_{0}^{\beta}d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2}\left(\Sigma(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})G(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})-\frac{J^{2}}{q}G(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})^{q}\right)\right]\,. $$

At large $N$ the asymptotic of the RHS of (12) is given by saddle points contributions

$$ \overline{Z_{\text{RD}}}=\exp\{-S_{RD}\} $$

where the saddle points of (12) are given by the Schwinger-Dyson equations for melonic diagrams [2, 3]

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{\partial_{\tau}-\hat{\Sigma}}=\hat{G}\,; \displaystyle\Sigma(\tau,\tau^{\prime})=J^{2}G(\tau,\tau^{\prime})^{q-1}\,, $$

where in the first equation hats denote the integral operators with the kernels defined by the corresponding bilocal fields.

The solutions of these equations in general case can be constructed numerically, which was done in the previous work [3, 4, 17, 12], and analytic solution is known in the IR/strong coupling limit $\beta J\gg 1$ .

#### 2.1.1 Strong coupling limit

Substituting (15) into (14) and taking $\partial_{\tau}\to 0$ , one obtains the equation

$$ J^{2}\int_{0}^{\beta}d\tau^{\prime}G(\tau,\tau^{\prime})G(\tau^{\prime},\tau^{\prime\prime})^{q-1}=-\delta(\tau-\tau^{\prime\prime})\,. $$

The solution for $G$ of the equation (16) has the form of the conformal propagator on the circle:

$$ g_{c,\beta}(\tau,\tau^{\prime})=b\left(\frac{\pi}{\beta}\right)^{2\Delta}\frac{\text{sgn}(\tau-\tau^{\prime})}{\left|\sin\frac{\pi}{\beta}(\tau-\tau^{\prime})\right|^{2\Delta}}\,, $$

where $\Delta=\frac{1}{q}$ is the conformal dimension of the Majorana fermion and

$$ b^{q}=\frac{(q-2)\tan\frac{\pi}{q}}{2\pi qJ^{2}}\,. $$

In the frequency space the conformal propagator on a circle has a form [30, 8]:

$$ \displaystyle g_{c,\beta}(\omega_{n})=-i2b\left(\frac{2\pi}{\beta}\right)^{2\Delta-1}\cos(\pi\Delta)\frac{\Gamma\left(\frac{\beta}{2\pi}\omega_{n}+\Delta\right)\Gamma(1-2\Delta)}{\Gamma\left(\frac{\beta}{2\pi}\omega_{n}+1-\Delta\right)}\;, $$

where $\omega_{n}$ are Matsubara frequencies:

$$ \omega_{n}=\frac{2\pi}{\beta}\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)\,,\quad n\in\mathbb{Z}\,. $$

At zero temperature (17) and (19) reduce to

$$ \displaystyle g_{c}(\tau) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{b}{|\tau|^{2\Delta}}\text{sgn}(\tau) \displaystyle g_{c}(\omega) \displaystyle= \displaystyle=ib\,2^{1-2\Delta}\sqrt{\pi}{\Gamma(1-\Delta)\over\Gamma({1\over 2}+\Delta)}|\omega|^{{2\Delta}-1}\text{sgn}(\omega)\,, $$

where $b$ is the dimensional constant fixed from (18). The equations (14), (15) are invariant under time reparametrizations $\tau\to f(\tau)$ in the strong coupling limit, provided the bilocal fields transform as follows (we assume without loss of generality that $f$ is a monotonically increasing function):

$$ \displaystyle G(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})=f^{\prime}(\tau_{1})^{\Delta}f^{\prime}(\tau_{2})^{\Delta}G(f(\tau_{1}),f(\tau_{2}))\,; \displaystyle\Sigma(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})=f^{\prime}(\tau_{1})^{1-\Delta}f^{\prime}(\tau_{2})^{1-\Delta}\Sigma(f(\tau_{1}),f(\tau_{2}))\,. $$

Acting with these transformations on the solution (17), one can generate the full infinite-dimensional manifold $\text{diff}(S^{1})/SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ of the replica-diagonal saddle points.

#### 2.1.2 On-shell action for replica-diagonal solution

The replica-diagonal on-shell action is given by

$$ \frac{2}{N}S_{RD}=\mathfrak{s}_{1}+\mathfrak{s}_{2}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\mathfrak{s}_{1} \displaystyle= \displaystyle-\text{Tr}\log\left(\partial_{\tau}-\hat{\Sigma}\right); \displaystyle\mathfrak{s}_{2} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\beta}\!\!\!\int_{0}^{\beta}d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2}\,\left(G(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\Sigma(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})-\frac{J^{2}}{q}G(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})^{q}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\left(1-\frac{1}{q}\right)J^{2}\int_{0}^{\beta}\!\!\!\int_{0}^{\beta}d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2}\,G(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})^{q}=\left(1-\frac{1}{q}\right)\text{Tr}({\bf 1}-\partial_{\tau}\hat{G})\,, $$

where $G$ and $\Sigma$ solve (14) and (15).

The conformal limit is obtained by neglecting the time derivative. The $s_{1}$ and $s_{2}$ can be simplified and we can rewrite them in the equivalent forms

$$ \displaystyle\mathfrak{s}_{1,c} \displaystyle= \displaystyle-\text{Tr}\log\left(-\hat{\Sigma}_{c}\right)=-\text{Tr}\log\left(-J^{2}\hat{g}_{c}^{q-1}\right) \displaystyle\mathfrak{s}_{2,c} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\left(1-\frac{1}{q}\right)J^{2}\int d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2}g_{c}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})^{q}=\left(1-\frac{1}{q}\right)\text{Tr}\,\,{\bf 1}. $$

In the conformal limit both these pieces in the on-shell action diverge and have to be regularized. It is expected that the renormalization can be performed pertrurbatively (in $1/\beta J$ ) by reinstating the time derivative in $\mathfrak{s}_{1}$ and evaluating the corresponding counterterms, and the resulting renormalized action equals to the on-shell action, evaluated on the solution of exact saddle point equations [3].

### 2.2 Nonperturbative nature of the replica-nondiagonal correlators

Here we will show that one cannot obtain a replica-nondiagonal large $N$ solution in perturbation theory over the free fermionic theory. We will work in the frequency space, and we also fix $q=4$ . In the free case we have $J=0$ , and the saddle point equations (8)-(9) are solved by

$$ G_{\alpha\beta}(\omega)=G_{f}(\omega)\delta_{\alpha\beta}\,; $$

where $G_{f}$ is defined from

$$ -i\omega G_{f}(\omega)=1\,. $$

We introduce the dimensionless parameter $\lambda$ and look for the solution by perturbing the free UV fixed point:

$$ G_{\alpha\beta}(\omega)=G_{f}(\omega)\delta_{\alpha\beta}+\lambda g^{(1)}_{\alpha\beta}(\omega)+\lambda^{2}g^{(2)}_{\alpha\beta}(\omega)+\dots,. $$

The field $\Sigma$ in this case is expanded as follows:

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}(\omega) \displaystyle= \displaystyle 3J^{2}\lambda(G_{f}*G_{f}*g^{(1)}_{\alpha\beta})(\omega)\delta_{\alpha\beta}+3J^{2}\lambda^{2}(G_{f}*g^{(1)}_{\alpha\beta}*g^{(1)}_{\alpha\beta})(\omega)\delta_{\alpha\beta} \displaystyle+ \displaystyle 3J^{2}\lambda^{2}(G_{f}*G_{f}*g^{(2)}_{\alpha\beta})(\omega)\delta_{\alpha\beta}+J^{2}\lambda(g^{(1)}_{\alpha\beta}*g^{(1)}_{\alpha\beta}*g^{(1)}_{\alpha\beta})(\omega)+\dots\,, $$

where the star denotes the functional contraction in the frequency space, and the replica matrices are always multiplied a-la Hadamard, i.e. component-wise. Note that the leading possible replica-nondiagonal contribution to $\Sigma$ is of order $\lambda^{q-1}$ . Substituting all this into the saddle point equation (8) and equating the powers of $\lambda$ , we arrive at an infinite system of linear inhomogeneous integral equations for $g^{(k)}$ . For example, for $\lambda^{1}$ we obtain

$$ i\omega g^{(1)}_{\alpha\beta}(\omega)=3J^{2}G_{f}(\omega)\ (G_{f}*G_{f}*g^{(1)}_{\alpha\beta})(\omega)\delta_{\alpha\beta}\,. $$

It is clear that the solution for $g^{(1)}$ of this equation is replica-diagonal. Having solved this equation, one can substitute the solution into the $\lambda^{2}$ equation, which would then allow to solve for $g^{(2)}$ . However, since everything in the equation will be replica-diagonal, the solution for $g^{(2)}$ will also be replica-diagonal. Using this expansion one can construct the solution up to any finite order in $\lambda$ , and it will thus always remain replica-diagonal, ultimately because the free fixed point $G_{f}$ is replica-diagonal44 4 Note that this argument does not rule out the replica-diagonal solutions with broken replica symmetry, i.e. different values of $g_{\alpha\alpha}$ for distinct $\alpha$ ..

This means that we cannot obtain a replica-nondiagonal solution as a low-energy limit of a replica-diagonal solution, and any replica-nondiagonal large $N$ solution would be nonperturbative in $(\beta J)^{-1}$ .

## 3 Nondiagonal saddles in the $q=2$ model

In this section we consider the $q=2$ variant of the SYK model. We present a class of simple exact replica-nondiagonal solutions and study their properties.

### 3.1 The solutions

Let us consider the $q=2$ case and show that there are replica-nondiagonal solutions of the saddle point equation. The saddle point equations (8)-(9) in the $q=2$ case condense to a single equation, which in terms of replica matrices is written as

$$ \displaystyle G(\omega)\cdot\Big(-i\omega\ I-J^{2}G(\omega)\Big) \displaystyle= \displaystyle I\,. $$

Here $G(\omega)=(G(\omega))_{\alpha\beta}$ is a $M\times M$ matrix, where $\omega$ is the Matsubara frequency, and $I$ is the unit matrix in the replica space. We assume the replica-symmetric ansatz

$$ G_{\alpha\alpha}=G_{0},\,\,\,\,\,G_{\alpha\beta}=G_{1},\,\,for\,\,\alpha\neq\beta,\,\,\,\,\,\alpha,\beta=1,...M $$

The equation (35) turns into the pair of equations for $G_{0}$ and $G_{1}$ :

$$ \displaystyle-i\omega G_{0}-J^{2}\Big(G_{0}^{2}+(M-1)G_{1}^{2}\Big) \displaystyle= \displaystyle 1 \displaystyle-i\omega G_{1}-J^{2}\Big(2G_{0}G_{1}+G_{1}^{2}(M-2)\Big) \displaystyle= \displaystyle 0 $$

In order to obtain the fermionic solutions, we have to impose the antisymmetry condition

$$ \displaystyle G_{\alpha\beta}(\omega) \displaystyle= \displaystyle-G_{\beta\alpha}(-\omega)\,, $$

which in terms of the replica-symmetric ansatz simply means that $G_{0}$ and $G_{1}$ have to be odd functions in frequency and time domains.

The equations (37)-(38) are readily solved. There are two replica-diagonal solutions:

$$ \displaystyle G_{0}^{(1)}(\omega) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{-i\omega+\,i\text{sgn}(\omega)\sqrt{4J^{2}+\omega^{2}}}{2J^{2}}\,; \displaystyle G_{0}^{(2)}(\omega) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{-i\omega-\,i\text{sgn}(\omega)\sqrt{4J^{2}+\omega^{2}}}{2J^{2}}\,; \displaystyle G_{1}^{(j)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle 0\,\,\,\,\,\mbox{for }\,\,j=1,2, $$

and two replica-nondiagonal solutions

$$ \displaystyle G_{0}^{(3)}(\omega) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{-i\omega+\,i\,\text{sgn}(\omega)\sqrt{4J^{2}+\omega^{2}}\left(1-\frac{2}{M}\right)}{2J^{2}}\,; \displaystyle G_{1}^{(3)}(\omega) \displaystyle= \displaystyle-\,i\,\text{sgn}(\omega)\frac{\sqrt{4J^{2}+\omega^{2}}}{J^{2}M}\,; \displaystyle G_{0}^{(4)}(\omega) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{-i\omega-\,i\,\text{sgn}(\omega)\sqrt{4J^{2}+\omega^{2}}\left(1-\frac{2}{M}\right)}{2J^{2}}\,; \displaystyle G_{1}^{(4)}(\omega) \displaystyle= \displaystyle i\,\text{sgn}(\omega)\frac{\sqrt{4J^{2}+\omega^{2}}}{J^{2}M}\,. $$

Let us make a few remarks about these solutions. The first solution coincides with the solution presented in [3]. It admits the $J=0$ limit, where its leading asymptotic is given by the free correlator $\frac{1}{-i\omega}$ . The second solution is the one, which gives subleading saddles, discussed by Cotler et al in [17]. All solutions are pure imaginary and

$$ \displaystyle\text{Re}\ G_{k}^{(j)}(\omega) \displaystyle= \displaystyle 0=\text{Re}\ G_{k}^{(j)}{(\omega)}\,; \displaystyle G_{k}^{(j)}(-\omega) \displaystyle= \displaystyle-G_{k}^{(j)}(\omega),\,\,\,G_{k}^{(j)*}(\omega)=-G_{k}^{(j)}(\omega)=G_{k}^{(j)}(-\omega),\,\,\,\,\,k=0,1 $$

There are also the relations

$$ \displaystyle G_{0}^{(3)}-G_{1}^{(3)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle G_{0}^{(1)}\,; \displaystyle G_{0}^{(4)}-G_{1}^{(4)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle G_{0}^{(2)}\,. $$

In regards to the replica-nondiagonal third and fourth solutions, the important property worth pointing out here is that they are singular in the $M\to 0$ limit. Also, one can check that these solutions are singular in the free limit $J\to 0$ , which confirms the nonperturbative nature of these solutions, discussed in the sec. 2.2. We will see that these properties remain for the class of numerical $q=4$ solutions that we studied.

We conclude this subsection with a comment about other solutions of the equation (35). This is a quadratic matrix equation, which means that in principle one can find and classify all of the solutions at any fixed $M$ . Their general form can be found by rewriting the equation (35) as follows55 5 We thank Andrey Mikhailov for pointing this out.:

$$ \displaystyle\left(JG(\omega)+\frac{i\omega}{2J}I\right)^{2}=-\left(1+\frac{\omega^{2}}{4J^{2}}\right)I\,. $$

The general solution will have a form

$$ \displaystyle G=-\frac{i\omega}{2J^{2}}I\pm i\frac{\sqrt{4J^{2}+\omega^{2}}}{2J^{2}}X\,; $$

where $X$ is a matrix which parametrizes a particular solution, such that:

$$ X\cdot X=I\,. $$

There is no explicit dependence on $M$ in (52), however the diagonal component of equation (53) has a sum of $M$ terms equal to $1$ . That means that the individual non-trivial components of $X$ should contain the $1/M$ dependence to compensate. Because of this argument, we expect that every solution will have singularity at $M\to 0$ .

However, in the subleading $\omega^{1}$ order and higher there is difference. As hinted by this asymptotic and confirmed by the plots of the exact expressions on Fig.1, the $M=1$ is a threshold value which distinguishes between two different types of behavior of saddle points:

- • $M>1$ . In this case $1-2/M>-1$ , so that the diagonal $1$ -st solution dominates, see Fig.1A,B.

Besides the observations mentioned above, from these density plots it is evident that the IR region seems to be more robust in the singular $M\to 0$ limit, rather than the UV. One can interpret this as a hint towards the fact that the singular behavior in $M\to 0$ limit of nondiagonal solutions is the UV effect in the SYK model. We explain more evidence for this in other sections of the paper.

## 4 Exact nondiagonal saddles in $q=4$ SYK: numerical study

Having found nondiagonal solutions in the $q=2$ model, we now turn to study the interacting $q=4$ model. In this case the saddle point equations (8)-(9) cannot be solved analytically in general, so we construct the solutions numerically. As was done in the previous section, we assume the replica-symmetric ansatz (36). In terms of independent variables the saddle point equations read

$$ \displaystyle-i\omega G_{0}(\omega)-G_{0}(\omega)\Sigma_{0}(\omega)-(M-1)G_{1}(\omega)\Sigma_{1}(\omega)=1\,; \displaystyle-i\omega G_{1}(\omega)-G_{1}(\omega)\Sigma_{0}(\omega)-G_{0}(\omega)\Sigma_{1}(\omega)-(M-2)G_{1}(\omega)\Sigma_{1}(\omega)=0\,; \displaystyle\Sigma_{0,1}(\tau,\tau^{\prime})=J^{2}G_{0,1}(\tau,\tau^{\prime})^{q-1}\,. $$

We solve the equations numerically at finite temperature, with $\beta=2\pi$ .

### 4.1 Comments on the method

We solve the system of integral equations (65)-(67) by iterating them. We use the approach employed in [17] in studies of subleading replica-diagonal saddles. The main idea is to start iterations with $q=2$ , using a particular solution of the $q=2$ model as a trial functions, and gradually increase $q$ from $2$ to $4$ during the procedure. Let us know discuss the procedure in more detail.

#### Initial condition.

The trial functions for $G_{0}$ and $G_{1}$ are constructed by choosing one of the four solutions (40)-(46) for every Matsubara frequency. We want the resulting solution in the interacting model to have the asymptotic behavior in the UV region that would correspond to the free theory, so we only consider the $q=2$ trial functions for which $\exists\bar{n}$ such that $G_{0,1}(\omega_{n})=-G_{0,1}(-\omega_{n})=G^{(1)}_{0,1}(\omega_{n})$ $\forall n\geq\bar{n}$ . In this case for any $n<\bar{n}$ we can choose $G_{0,1}(\omega_{n})=-G_{0,1}(-\omega_{n})$ to be equal to any of the four solutions (40)-(46).

#### Iteration procedure.

We divide the iterations into two stages.

- 1. We start first stage of iterations at $q=2$ . At each iteration, $q$ is increased by some small amount. At every step $\Sigma_{0}$ and $\Sigma_{1}$ are computed in the position space using fast Fourier transform for $G$ and equation (67), and then the inverse fast Fourier transform is performed on $\Sigma_{0,1}$ . Then $G_{0}(\omega)$ and $G_{1}(\omega)$ are updated according to the weighted rule (as also used in [3]) of the form

$$ G_{0,1}^{\text{new}}=(1-x)\ G_{0,1}+x\ \tilde{G}_{0,1}\,, $$

(68) where $0<x<1$ is the weighting coefficient and $\tilde{G}$ is defined by solving the equations (65)-(66) in terms of $G_{0}$ and $G_{1}$ : $\displaystyle\tilde{G}_{0}$ $\displaystyle=$ $\displaystyle\frac{1}{-i\omega_{n}-\Sigma_{0}+\Sigma_{1}}+\frac{\Sigma_{1}}{(i\omega_{n}+\Sigma_{0}-\Sigma_{1})(i\omega_{n}+\Sigma_{0}+(M-1)\Sigma_{1})}\,;$ (69) $\displaystyle\tilde{G}_{1}$ $\displaystyle=$ $\displaystyle\frac{\Sigma_{1}}{(i\omega_{n}+\Sigma_{0}-\Sigma_{1})(i\omega_{n}+\Sigma_{0}+(M-1)\Sigma_{1})}\,.$ (70) At this stage we keep the weight fixed, and the procedure is finished when $q$ reaches $4$ .

- 2. The second stage of iterations is performed at fixed $q=4$ . Its purpose is to tune the solutions, obtained in the previous stage, to the desired precision. In this procedure we take the approach of [3] and control the $\mathcal{L}_{2}$ -norm of the solutions between successive steps

$$ ||\Delta G_{0,1}||^{2}=\int_{0}^{\beta}d\tau|G_{0,1}(\tau)^{\text{new}}-G_{0,1}(\tau)^{\text{old}}|^{2}\,, $$

(71) decreasing the weight $x$ every time the $||\Delta G_{0,1}||^{2}$ starts increasing. The procedure is completed once $||\Delta G_{0,1}||^{2}$ reaches zero (up to desired numerical accuracy).

The main limitation of our approach is that only real-valued stable numerical solutions can be obtained. This puts limitations on making connections with the analytic solutions in the conformal limit, which we discuss in the section 5) and thereafter.

### 4.2 The results

When studying the saddle points of the replica partition function at finite $M$ , the obtained solutions indicate that for every $q=2$ solution, that we choose as initial condition as discussed above, there exists a solution of the $q=4$ model. This generalizes the observation, made in [17] for the replica-diagonal solutions, to the replica-nondiagonal symmetric case. The solutions shown on Fig.3 are obtained by iterating from the following $q=2$ solutions:

- A. $M=4$ . $G_{0,1}(\omega_{0})=-G_{0,1}(\omega_{-1})=G_{0,1}^{(3)}(\omega_{0})$ ; $G_{0,1}(\omega_{n})=G_{0,1}^{(1)}(\omega_{n})$ for all other $n$ .

- B. $M=4$ . $G_{0,1}(\omega_{1})=-G_{0,1}(\omega_{-2})=G_{0,1}^{(3)}(\omega_{1})$ ; $G_{0}(\omega_{n})=G_{0}^{(1)}(\omega_{n})$ for all other $n$ .

- C. $M=4$ . $G_{0,1}(\omega_{4})=-G_{0,1}(\omega_{-5})=G_{0,1}^{(3)}(\omega_{4})$ ; $G_{0,1}(\omega_{n})=G_{0,1}^{(1)}(\omega_{n})$ for all other $n$ .

- D. $M=2$ . $G_{0,1}(\omega_{0})=-G_{0,1}(\omega_{-1})=G_{0,1}^{(3)}(\omega_{0})$ ; $G_{0,1}(\omega_{n})=G_{0,1}^{(1)}(\omega_{n})$ for all other $n$ .

- E. $M=2$ . $G_{0,1}(\omega_{1})=-G_{0,1}(\omega_{-2})=G_{0,1}^{(3)}(\omega_{1})$ ; $G_{0}(\omega_{n})=G_{0}^{(1)}(\omega_{n})$ for all other $n$ .

- F. $M=2$ . $G_{0,1}(\omega_{4})=-G_{0,1}(\omega_{-5})=G_{0,1}^{(3)}(\omega_{4})$ ; $G_{0,1}(\omega_{n})=G_{0,1}^{(1)}(\omega_{n})$ for all other $n$ .

- G. $M=2$ . $G_{0,1}(\omega_{0})=-G_{0,1}(\omega_{-1})=G_{0,1}^{(4)}(\omega_{0})$ ; $G_{0,1}(\omega_{n})=G_{0,1}^{(1)}(\omega_{n})$ for all other $n$ .

- H. $M=2$ . $G_{0,1}(\omega_{1})=-G_{0,1}(\omega_{-2})=G_{0,1}^{(4)}(\omega_{1})$ ; $G_{0}(\omega_{n})=G_{0}^{(1)}(\omega_{n})$ for all other $n$ .

- I. $M=0.5$ . $G_{0,1}(\omega_{4})=-G_{0,1}(\omega_{-5})=G_{0,1}^{(4)}(\omega_{4})$ ; $G_{0,1}(\omega_{n})=G_{0,1}^{(1)}(\omega_{n})$ for all other $n$ .

- J. $M=0.5$ . $G_{0,1}(\omega_{0})=-G_{0,1}(\omega_{-1})=G_{0,1}^{(3)}(\omega_{0})$ ; $G_{0,1}(\omega_{n})=G_{0,1}^{(1)}(\omega_{n})$ for all other $n$ .

- K. $M=0.5$ . $G_{0,1}(\omega_{1})=-G_{0,1}(\omega_{-2})=G_{0,1}^{(3)}(\omega_{1})$ ; $G_{0}(\omega_{n})=G_{0}^{(1)}(\omega_{n})$ for all other $n$ .

- L. $M=0.5$ . $G_{0,1}(\omega_{4})=-G_{0,1}(\omega_{-5})=G_{0,1}^{(3)}(\omega_{4})$ ; $G_{0,1}(\omega_{n})=G_{0,1}^{(1)}(\omega_{n})$ for all other $n$ .

We have also studied this class of solutions in the limit $M\to 0$ . For this purpose we add a third stage of iterations, where we keep $q$ fixed, but change the value of $M$ from some finite initial value to zero during iterations. Evaluating $||\Delta G_{0,1}||^{2}$ and the left hand side of the equations of motion, we observe that the sequence of functions obtained this way fails to converge to any solution of the saddle point equations, other than the standard replica-diagonal saddle. When starting from a replica-nondiagonal solution at finite $M$ , we observe that the iterated functions develop discontinuities as $M\to 0$ . Thus, from our numerical evidence we conclude that the singular behavior in the $M\to 0$ limit, that we see in the analytic $q=2$ solutions, persists for nondiagonal solutions in the $q=4$ model. Therefore, the main result of our numerical investigation is that at finite replica number we get an infinite number of nontrivial replica-nondiagonal saddle points, whereas in zero replicas limit we do not obtain any replica-nondiagonal solutions of the exact saddle point equations.
