Definition. The Parisi matrix $Q$ associated with the given tree $\mathfrak{T}$ with a set $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathfrak{T}}$ is defined as follows

$$ \displaystyle Q_{a,a} \displaystyle= \displaystyle q_{0}, \displaystyle Q_{a,b} \displaystyle= \displaystyle Q_{b,a}=q_{i},\,\,\,\text{if}\,\,\,\left\{\begin{array}[]{ccc}\Big[\frac{a-1}{m_{i}}\Big]&\neq&\Big[\frac{b-1}{m_{i}}\Big]\\
&\text{and}&\\
\Big[\frac{a-1}{m_{i+1}}\Big]&=&\Big[\frac{b-1}{m_{i+1}}\Big]\end{array}\right\} \displaystyle a,b=1,...,M $$

### A.2 Representation in terms of block matrices $\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}}$

It is convenient to represent the Parisi matrix (252) using the family of the block matrices $\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}}$ composed on 1’s and 0’s

$$ \mathcal{I}_{m_{i}}=I_{M/m_{i}}\otimes\mathfrak{J}_{m_{i}} $$

Here $\mathfrak{J}_{l}$ are Hadamard identity matrices of dimension $m_{i}$ :

$$ (\mathfrak{J}_{i})_{kj}=1\,,\quad k,j=1,\dots,m_{i}\,. $$

and $I_{p}$ are the usual unit matrix of dimension $p$ , $\otimes$ is the tensor product. The matrix $Q$ defined by (252) can be represented as

$$ Q=\sum_{i=1,\,\,m_{i}\in\mathfrak{T}}^{l}\,q_{i}(\mathcal{I}_{m_{i+1}}-\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}})+q_{0}\mathcal{I}_{1} $$

Note that in according with (253)

$$ \mathcal{I}_{m_{1}}\equiv\mathcal{I}_{1}=\mathfrak{J}_{1}\otimes I_{M}=I_{M} $$

Notice that representation (255) is equivalent to the following representation

$$ \displaystyle Q \displaystyle= \displaystyle q_{0}\mathcal{I}_{1}+q_{1}(\mathcal{I}_{m_{2}}-\mathcal{I}_{m_{1}})+q_{2}(\mathcal{I}_{m_{3}}-\mathcal{I}_{m_{2}})+...+q_{l}(\mathcal{I}_{m_{l+1}}-\mathcal{I}_{m_{l}}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle(q_{0}-q_{1}){I}_{M}+(q_{1}-q_{2})\mathcal{I}_{m_{2}}+(q_{2}-q_{3})\mathcal{I}_{m_{3}}+...+(q_{l-1}-q_{l})\mathcal{I}_{m_{l}}+q_{l}\mathfrak{J}_{M}\,, $$

where we use (256) and

$$ \mathcal{I}_{m_{l+1}}=\mathfrak{J}_{M}\,. $$

Rewriting (257) we get

$$ \displaystyle Q \displaystyle= \displaystyle(q_{0}-q_{1})\mathcal{I}_{1}+\sum_{i=1}^{l-1}(q_{i}-q_{i+1})\mathcal{I}_{m_{i+1}}+q_{l}\mathfrak{J}_{M} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{l-1}(q_{i}-q_{i+1})\mathcal{I}_{m_{i+1}}+q_{l}\mathfrak{J}_{M} $$

### A.3 Algebra of Parisi matrices

The block matrices $\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}}$ satisfy the following relations

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}}=\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}}\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}}=m_{i}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}},\,\,\,\mbox{for}\,\,\,\,i\leq j $$

From this statement follow the

#### Lemma.

The space of Parisi matrices with fixed tree $\mathfrak{T}\{r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}...r_{l}\}$ is an algebra under both regular and Hadamard matrix products.

Proof. The closeness under the Hadamard product is obvious. For the direct matrix product this follows from representation (255) and the following properties (260) of $\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}}$ matrices corresponding to the same tree. Indeed we define the two Parisi matrices of the rank $l$ ( $a_{l+1}=0$ ):

$$ \displaystyle A=\sum_{i=1,\,\,m_{i}\in\mathfrak{T}}^{l}\,a_{i}(\mathcal{I}_{m_{i+1}}-\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}})+q_{0}\mathcal{I}_{1}\,; \displaystyle B=\sum_{i=1,\,\,m_{i}\in\mathfrak{T}}^{l}\,b_{i}(\mathcal{I}_{m_{i+1}}-\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}})+b_{0}\mathcal{I}_{1}\,. $$

We want to calculate their product, which we denote as

$$ W=A\cdot B\,. $$

We proceed as follows:

$$ \displaystyle W=a_{0}b_{0}\mathcal{I}_{1}+\sum_{i}(b_{0}a_{i}+a_{0}b_{i})(\mathcal{I}_{m_{i+1}}-\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}})+\text{four terms}\,. $$

The four terms come from the multiplication of two brackets between each other. Let us evaluate carefully each term using the relation (260). The first term gives

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{T}_{1}:=\sum_{i}\sum_{j}a_{i}b_{j}\mathcal{I}_{m_{i+1}}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}=\sum_{j}\sum_{i<j}a_{i}b_{j}m_{i+1}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}+\sum_{j}a_{j}b_{j}m_{j+1}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}+\sum_{j}\sum_{i>j}a_{i}b_{j}m_{j+1}\mathcal{I}_{m_{i+1}} \displaystyle=\sum_{j}\sum_{i<j}(a_{i}b_{j}+a_{j}b_{i})m_{i+1}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}+\sum_{j}a_{j}b_{j}m_{j+1}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}\,. $$

The second term yields

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{T}_{2}:=-\sum_{i}\sum_{j}a_{i}b_{j}\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}=-\sum_{j}\sum_{i<j+1}a_{i}b_{j}m_{i}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}-\sum_{j}a_{j+1}b_{j}m_{j+1}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}-\sum_{j}\sum_{i>j+1}a_{i}b_{j}m_{j+1}\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}} \displaystyle\!\!\!\!\!\!=-\sum_{j}\sum_{i<j}a_{i}b_{j}m_{i}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}-\sum_{j}a_{j}b_{j}m_{j}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}-\sum_{j}\sum_{i<j}a_{j}b_{i}m_{i+1}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}}\,. $$

We relabeled some summation indices and canceled two terms here. The third term can be obtained from $T_{2}$ by making the replacement $a\leftrightarrow b$ :

$$ \mathrm{T}_{3}:=-\sum_{i}\sum_{j}a_{i}b_{j}\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}+1}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}}=-\sum_{j}\sum_{i<j}b_{i}a_{j}m_{i}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}-\sum_{j=i}a_{j}b_{j}m_{j}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}-\sum_{j}\sum_{i<j}b_{j}a_{i}m_{i+1}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}}\,. $$

The fourth term yields:

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{T}_{4}: \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{i}\sum_{j}a_{i}b_{j}\mathcal{I}_{m_{i}}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}}=\sum_{j}\sum_{i<j}a_{i}b_{j}m_{i}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}}+\sum_{j=i}a_{j}b_{j}m_{j}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}}+\sum_{j}\sum_{i<j}a_{j}b_{i}m_{i}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{j}\sum_{i<j}(a_{i}b_{j}+a_{j}b_{i})m_{i}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}}+\sum_{j=i}a_{j}b_{j}m_{j}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}} $$

where we again relabeled the indices in the last term. Therefore, we have presented the four terms as a linear combination of the $\mathcal{I}$ -matrices, more specifically

$$ \text{four terms}=\sum_{j}(U_{j}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}+V_{j}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}})\,. $$

As it will become clear below, this is already proves the lemma. Let us write down the $U$ and $V$ explicitly:

$$ \displaystyle U_{j}=\sum_{i<j}(a_{i}b_{j}+b_{i}a_{j})(m_{i+1}-m_{i})+a_{j}b_{j}(m_{j+1}-2m_{j})\,. \displaystyle V_{j}=-\sum_{i<j}(a_{i}b_{j}+b_{i}a_{j})(m_{i+1}-m_{i})+a_{j}b_{j}m_{j}\,. $$

As we see, there is a difference between the two:

$$ D_{j}:=U_{j}+V_{j}=a_{j}b_{j}(m_{j+1}-m_{j})\,, $$

and therefore in $W$ there is a rogue term

$$ \sum_{j}D_{j}\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}} $$

However, we can deal with it using a trivial formula:

$$ \mathcal{I}_{m_{k}}=\mathcal{I}_{1}+\sum_{j<k}(\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}-\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}})\,. $$

Thus, we can write the term as follows:

$$ \sum_{i}D_{i}\mathcal{I}_{m_{i+1}}=\sum_{i}D_{i}\mathcal{I}_{1}+\sum_{i}\sum_{j<i+1}D_{i}(\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}-\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}})=\sum_{i}D_{i}\mathcal{I}_{1}+\sum_{j}\sum_{i>j-1}D_{i}(\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}-\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}})\,. $$

Therefore, the lemma is proved. We obtain that $W$ is a Parisi matrix

$$ W=\sum_{j}w_{j}(\mathcal{I}_{m_{j+1}}-\mathcal{I}_{m_{j}})+w_{0}\mathcal{I}_{1}\,, $$

where its parameters are given by

$$ \displaystyle w_{0} \displaystyle= \displaystyle a_{0}b_{0}+\sum_{j}a_{j}b_{j}(m_{j+1}-m_{j}); \displaystyle w_{j} \displaystyle= \displaystyle b_{0}a_{j}+a_{0}b_{j}+\sum_{i<j}(a_{i}b_{j}+b_{i}a_{j})(m_{i+1}-m_{i})-a_{j}b_{j}m_{j}+\sum_{i>j-1}a_{i}b_{i}(m_{i+1}-m_{i}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle b_{0}a_{j}+a_{0}b_{j}+\sum_{i<j}(a_{i}b_{j}+b_{i}a_{j})(m_{i+1}-m_{i})-a_{j}b_{j}m_{j}+\sum_{i>j}a_{i}b_{i}(m_{i+1}-m_{i}) \displaystyle+ \displaystyle a_{j}b_{j}(m_{j+1}-m_{j})\,. $$

∎ These formulae can be used to directly solve the equation (93), if one takes $b_{j}=a_{j}^{q-1}$ .

### A.4 Determinant of the Parisi matrix

The eigenvalues of the Parisi matrix $Q$ are given by the formulae [41]

$$ \displaystyle\lambda_{0} \displaystyle= \displaystyle q_{0}-q_{1} \displaystyle\lambda_{i} \displaystyle= \displaystyle q_{0}-q_{1}+\sum_{j=1}^{i}(q_{j}-q_{j+1})m_{j},\,\,\,\,\,\,i=1,2,...,l-1 \displaystyle\lambda_{l} \displaystyle= \displaystyle q_{0}-q_{1}+\sum_{j=1}^{l-1}(q_{j}-q_{j+1})m_{j}+q_{l}m_{l}. $$

Throughout the paper we compute $\log\det Q$ for different Parisi matrices both at finite and zero $M$ . We illustrate the calculation for $l=1$ and present the result for general $l$ .

In the case of $l=1$ , the determinant for arbitrary $M$ reads:

$$ \det Q=(q_{0}-q_{1})^{M-1}(q_{0}+(M-1)q_{1})\,. $$

For the logarithm we write

$$ \displaystyle\log\det Q=(M-1)\log(q_{0}-q_{1})+\log(q_{0}-q_{1})+\log\left(1+\frac{Mq_{1}}{q_{0}-q_{1}}\right) \displaystyle=M\log(q_{0}-q_{1})+\log\left(1+\frac{Mq_{1}}{q_{0}-q_{1}}\right)\,. $$

Taking the limit $M\to 0$ , we arrive at the expression

$$ \lim_{M\to 0}\frac{1}{M}\log\det Q=\log(q_{0}-q_{1})+\frac{q_{1}}{q_{0}-q_{1}}\,. $$

The cases of higher $l$ can be calculated analogously. The main idea is to extract the part from the lowest degree bracket which is the same as the next degree bracket, which will always be of the odd degree and carry a singular contribution.

For arbitrary $l$ we obtain the expression

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{M\to 0}\frac{1}{M}\log\det Q \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\log(q_{0}-q_{1})+\sum_{i=2}^{l-1}\frac{1}{2^{i}}\log(q_{0}+\sum_{m=0}^{i-1}2^{m}q_{m+2}-2^{i}q_{i+1}) \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2^{k-1}}\log(q_{0}+\sum_{m=0}^{l-1}2^{m}q_{m+2}-2^{l}q_{l})+\frac{1}{2}\frac{q_{l}}{q_{0}+\sum_{m=0}^{l-1}2^{m}q_{m+2}-2^{l}q_{l}}\,. $$

## Appendix B The action on replica-nondiagonal solutions at finite $M$

We start with the on-shell action for the path integral (6) at finite $M$ :

$$ \frac{2}{N}S_{M}=-\text{Tr}\log\left(\delta_{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\tau}-\hat{\Sigma}_{\alpha\beta}\right)+\int_{0}^{\beta}\int_{0}^{\beta}d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2}\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\left(G_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})-\frac{J^{2}}{q}G_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})^{q}\right)\Big|_{\text{on-shell}}\,. $$

We use the saddle point equations (8),(9) and rewrite it as

$$ \displaystyle\frac{2}{N}S_{M} \displaystyle= \displaystyle-\text{Tr}\log[\delta_{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\tau}-\hat{\Sigma}_{\alpha\beta}]+\left(1-\frac{1}{q}\right)J^{2}\int_{0}^{\beta}\int_{0}^{\beta}d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2}\sum_{\alpha,\beta}G_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})^{q}\Big|_{\text{on-shell}}\,. $$

We renormalize the logarithmic term by subtracting the free part $-M\text{Tr}\log(\partial_{\tau})$ [4, 3] and denote it as:

$$ \mathfrak{s}_{1}=-\text{Tr}\log\det\left(\delta_{\alpha\beta}+\frac{\hat{\Sigma}_{\alpha\beta}}{-\partial_{\tau}}\right)\Big|_{\text{on-shell}}\,, $$

where the determinant is taken over the replica indices. We denote the polynomial term as

$$ \mathfrak{s}_{2}=\left(1-\frac{1}{q}\right)J^{2}\int_{0}^{\beta}\int_{0}^{\beta}d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2}\sum_{\alpha,\beta}G_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})^{q}\Big|_{\text{on-shell}}\,. $$

#### Replica-symmetric ansatz.

In this case we have two dynamical variables $G_{0,1}$ (and corresponding $\Sigma_{0,1}(\tau)=J^{2}G_{0,1}^{q-1}(\tau)$ ). To evauate the Pfaffian term in the frequency space we use the formula for the determinant of a Parisi matrix (284) for every frequency:

$$ \log\det\left(\delta_{\alpha\beta}+\frac{\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}(\omega)}{i\omega}\right)=M\log\left(1+\frac{\Sigma_{0}(\omega)}{i\omega}-\frac{\Sigma_{1}(\omega)}{i\omega}\right)+\log\left(1+M\frac{\Sigma_{1}(\omega)}{i\omega+\Sigma_{0}(\omega)-\Sigma_{1}(\omega)}\right)\,. $$

At zero temperature, $\mathfrak{s}_{1}$ reads

$$ \mathfrak{s}_{1}=-\frac{\mathcal{V}}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\omega\left[M\log\left(1+\frac{\Sigma_{0}(\omega)}{i\omega}-\frac{\Sigma_{1}(\omega)}{i\omega}\right)+\log\left(1+M\frac{\Sigma_{1}(\omega)}{i\omega+\Sigma_{0}(\omega)-\Sigma_{1}(\omega)}\right)\right]\,. $$

At finite temperature we have instead the sum over Matsubara frequencies (20):

$$ \mathfrak{s}_{1}=-\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}\left[M\log\left(1+\frac{\Sigma_{0}(\omega_{n})}{i\omega_{n}}-\frac{\Sigma_{1}(\omega_{n})}{i\omega_{n}}\right)+\log\left(1+M\frac{\Sigma_{1}(\omega_{n})}{i\omega_{n}+\Sigma_{0}(\omega_{n})-\Sigma_{1}(\omega_{n})}\right)\right]\,. $$

For the polynomial term, we have the expression

$$ \mathfrak{s}_{2}=\left(1-\frac{1}{q}\right)J^{2}\int d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2}\left(MG_{0}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})^{q}+M(M-1)G_{1}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})^{q}\right)\,. $$

## Appendix C Observables and disorder: annealed vs quenched

Having found replica-nondiagonal solutions in $q=2$ and $q=4$ SYK models, it is appropriate to discuss which observables will be affected by these saddle points. For this purpose, it is useful to review the two types of correlation functions, which one can consider in a disordered model.

First, let us remind that the Lagrangian of the SYK model is given by [7, 3, 4]

$$ L[\psi,{\bf j}]=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\psi_{i}\frac{d}{d\tau}\psi_{i}-\frac{i^{q/2}}{q!}\sum_{i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{q}}j_{i_{1}i_{2}\dots\char 16\relax_{q}}\psi_{i_{1}}\psi_{i_{2}}\dots\psi_{i_{q}}\,, $$

which is used to construct the generating functional of SYK correlation functions for a fixed realization of disorder ${\bf j}=\{j_{i_{1}i_{2}\dots\char 16\relax_{q}}\}$ :

$$ Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;\eta)=\int D\psi\exp\left[-\int_{0}^{\beta}d\tau L[\psi,{\bf j}]+\int_{0}^{\beta}\eta_{i}(\tau)\psi_{i}(\tau)d\tau\right]\,. $$

Here we have introduced the fermionic sources $\eta_{i}(\tau)$ . The correlation functions in a fixed realization of disorder are defined as usual:

$$ \langle\psi_{i_{1}}(\tau_{1})\dots\psi_{i_{k}}(\tau_{k})\rangle_{{\bf j}}=\frac{1}{Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;0)}\frac{1}{k!}\left.\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta_{i_{1}}(\tau_{1})}\dots\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta_{i_{k}}(\tau_{k})}Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;\eta)\right|_{\eta=0}\,. $$

As a final preliminary remark, the average over the disorder of a function $f({\bf j})$ is performed by taking the integral

$$ \overline{f({\bf j})}=\int d{\bf j}\ P({\bf j})f({\bf j})\,, $$

where the Gaussian distribution $P({\bf j})$ is given by (2).

### C.1 Quenched quantities

In the quenched quantities the disorder averaging is performed on the last step. The quenched correlators are defined as

$$ \overline{\langle\psi_{i_{1}}(\tau_{1})\dots\psi_{i_{k}}(\tau_{k})\rangle}=\overline{\frac{1}{Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;0)}\frac{1}{k!}\left.\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta_{i_{1}}(\tau_{1})}\dots\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta_{i_{k}}(\tau_{k})}Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;\eta)\right|_{\eta=0}}\,. $$

Because the nominator and denominator are averaged together, these quantities require replica trick, and specifically they require taking the limit $M\to 0$ . Below we explicitly derive the representation of the quenched correlators in terms of the bilocal replica field path integral.

#### C.1.1 Replica-diagonal case

We start with the singlet two-point function of fermions in a single copy of SYK1313 13 We also emphasize the $N$ dependence for purposes of the further discussion:

$$ \mathcal{G}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N):=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overline{\langle\psi_{i}(\tau_{1})\psi_{i}(\tau_{2})\rangle}=\frac{1}{2!N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overline{\frac{1}{Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;0)}\left.\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta_{i}(\tau_{1})}\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta_{i}(\tau_{2})}Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;\eta)\right|_{\eta=0}}\,. $$

Now let us derive the expression for $\mathcal{G}$ in terms of the disorder-averaged bilocal replica field path integral. Let us define the bilocal field correlator in the disorder-averaged SYK with $M$ replicas:

$$ \displaystyle\mathfrak{G}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N,M) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int\prod_{\alpha,\beta=1}^{M}DG_{\alpha\beta}D\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}\ \mathrm{e}^{-NS[G_{\alpha\beta},\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}]}G_{MM}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\,. $$

In terms of this quantity, the quenched correlator is written as following:

$$ \mathcal{G}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N)=\lim_{M\to 0}\mathfrak{G}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N,M)\,. $$

Let us sketch the proof. On the first step we take the derivatives in (300) and write the nominator partition function explicitly as the path integral. For the normalizing denominator, we use the following formal identity [29]:

$$ Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;0)^{-1}=\lim_{M\to 0}Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;0)^{M-1}\,. $$

We get (the summation over color indices is implicit)

$$ \mathcal{G}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N)=\frac{1}{N}\overline{\lim_{M\to 0}Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;0)^{M-1}\int D\psi^{M}\ \mathrm{e}^{-S_{\text{SYK}}[{\bf j},\psi^{M}]}\psi_{i}^{M}(\tau_{1})\psi_{i}^{M}(\tau_{2})}\,, $$

where we have assigned a replica index $M$ to fermion fields participating in the last path integral. We can rewrite this as the path integral over $M$ replicas with insertions supported on the $M$ -th replica:

$$ \mathcal{G}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N)=\frac{1}{N}\overline{\lim_{M\to 0}\int\prod_{\alpha=1}^{M}D\psi^{\alpha}\ \mathrm{e}^{-\sum_{\alpha=1}^{M}S_{\text{SYK}}[{\bf j},\psi^{\alpha}]}\psi_{i}^{M}(\tau_{1})\psi_{i}^{M}(\tau_{2})}\,, $$

The averaging over the disorder can be performed in this replica integral in the same way as in the partition function (6). After that, we can rewrite this in terms of the bilocal fields with the fermions integrated out: 1414 14 This identity holds up to some numerical constants which come from the measure [4], which we omit:

$$ \overline{\int\prod_{\alpha^{\prime}=1}^{M}D\psi^{\alpha^{\prime}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-\sum_{\alpha^{\prime}=1}^{M}S_{\text{SYK}}[{\bf j},\psi^{\alpha^{\prime}}]}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\psi_{i}^{M}(\tau_{1})\psi_{i}^{M}(\tau_{2})}=\int\prod_{\alpha,\beta=1}^{M}DG_{\alpha\beta}D\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}\ \mathrm{e}^{-NS[G_{\alpha\beta},\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}]}G_{MM}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\,. $$

Thus, we obtain the formula (302):

$$ \mathcal{G}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N)=\lim_{M\to 0}\int\prod_{\alpha,\beta=1}^{M}DG_{\alpha\beta}D\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}\ \mathrm{e}^{-NS[G_{\alpha\beta},\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}]}G_{MM}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\,. $$

We see that a quenched correlator is expressed in terms of replica correlators in the limit $M\to 0$ . Note that this limit is taken before the thermodynamic limit $N\to\infty$ .

#### C.1.2 Replica-offdiagonal case

A common diagonostic of the spin glass physics is the quenched replica-offdiagonal correlator [24, 6, 1, 20, 35, 28, 21, 34]. Let us start with the two replicas $\alpha$ and $\beta$ of the given system. The offdiagonal quenched correlator is defined as

$$ \mathcal{G}_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N):=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overline{\langle\psi_{i}^{\alpha}(\tau_{1})\psi^{\beta}_{i}(\tau_{2})\rangle}=\frac{1}{2!N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overline{\frac{1}{Z^{(2)}_{{\bf j}}(\beta;0)}\left.\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta^{\alpha}_{i}(\tau_{1})}\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta^{\beta}_{i}(\tau_{2})}Z_{{\bf j}}^{(2)}(\beta;\eta^{\alpha},\eta^{\beta})\right|_{\eta=0}}\,. $$

Here $Z^{(2)}$ is the two-replica partition function. If the two replicas are independent, then $Z^{(2)}_{\bf j}(\beta;\eta^{\alpha},\eta^{\beta})=Z_{\bf j}(\beta;\eta^{\alpha})Z_{\bf j}(\beta;\eta^{\beta})$ and the expression under line can factorizes into product of two one-point functions:

$$ \overline{\frac{1}{Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;0)^{2}}\left.\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta^{\alpha}_{i}(\tau_{1})}\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta^{\beta}_{i}(\tau_{2})}Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;\eta^{\alpha})Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;\eta^{\beta})\right|_{\eta=0}}=\overline{\langle\psi_{i}^{\alpha}(\tau_{1})\rangle\langle\psi_{i}^{\beta}(\tau_{1})\rangle}\,. $$

In the fermionic theory, like SYK, the one-point functions vanish, which, assuming $N$ is finite, gives that in total $\mathcal{G}_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})=0$ 1515 15 This argument does not generally work in the thermodynamic limit $N\to\infty$ .. This is a general argument that is often presented to support the absense of spin glass phase in fermionic models such as variations of SY and SYK [24, 1, 20, 35, 21].

Let us now see what this tells us about the replica structure of the $G$ , $\Sigma$ saddle points. We again define the replica bilocal field correlator

$$ \displaystyle\mathfrak{G}_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N,M) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int\prod_{\alpha,\beta=1}^{M}DG_{\alpha\beta}D\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}\ \mathrm{e}^{-NS[G_{\alpha\beta},\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}]}G_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\,,\quad\alpha\neq\beta\,. $$

Note that, formally speaking, $\mathfrak{G}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N,M)=\mathfrak{G}_{MM}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N,M)$ (see (301)). Analogously to the diagonal case (302), one can derive the bilocal field representation for the quenched offdiagonal correlator:

$$ \mathcal{G}_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N)=\lim_{M\to 0}\mathfrak{G}_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N,M)\,. $$

The proof goes as follows. Proceeding analogously to the derivation of the expression (302) above, we write

$$ \mathcal{G}_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N)=\frac{1}{N}\overline{\lim_{M\to 0}Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;0)^{M-2}\int D\psi^{\alpha}D\psi^{\beta}\ \mathrm{e}^{-S_{\text{SYK}}[{\bf j},\psi^{\alpha}]-S_{\text{SYK}}[{\bf j},\psi^{\beta}]}\psi_{i}^{\alpha}(\tau_{1})\psi_{i}^{\beta}(\tau_{2})}\,, $$

or in terms of the disorder-averaged replica bilocal field theory we obtain

$$ \mathcal{G}_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N)=\lim_{M\to 0}\int\prod_{\gamma,\delta=1}^{M}DG_{\gamma\delta}D\Sigma_{\gamma\delta}\ \mathrm{e}^{-NS[G_{\gamma\delta},\Sigma_{\gamma\delta}]}G_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\,. $$

This formula gives representation for non-diagonal disorder correlator in terms of the disorder-averaged replica bilocal field theory. We once again see that the quenched correlator is governed by the replica structure in the limit $M\to 0$ .

The replica factorization and vanishing of the fermionic one-point functions at large (but finite) $N$ seems to tell that there should be no replica-nondiagonal saddle points, but in fact this is not conclusive. It is worth noting that the factorization argument holds at finite $N$ , and it does not exclude possible dominant non-diagonal saddle points in the thermodynamic limit $N\to\infty$ . The factorization adds a nontrivial nonperturbative constraint on the full $1/N$ expansion of the right hand side of (311). In particular, at some orders of $1/N$ one expects replica-nondiagonal contributions in perturbations even over the replica-diagonal saddle [35, 16, 4]. The factorization in the fermionic case implies that all such perturbative corrections should resum to zero, together with any nonperturbative corrections (that come e.g. from subleading saddles). Of course, with only finite amount of the asymptotic $1/N$ series taken into account, one does not expect zero. This will be more relevant to our results in the case of annealed correlators.

### C.2 Annealed quantities

The quantities, which are obtained by performing annealed averaging, treat the disorder on equal footing with other microscopic degrees of freedom of the model. In the general case, one can also consider annealed quantities that deal with $M$ copies of the initial model by construction. The simplest example is the replica partition function $\overline{Z(\beta)^{M}}$ , which we consider throughout the paper, taken with an integer $M$ . As we show in sections 3 and 4, there are nontrivial exact replica-nondiagonal saddle points, contributing to this quantity in case of a finite replica number. We also show that these saddle points are suppressed at large $N$ , giving nonperturbative contributions to the $1/N$ -expansion that are suppressed exponentially like $\mathrm{e}^{-NS}$ .

Another closely related example of an annealed quantity is the spectral form factor $\frac{1}{\overline{Z(\beta)^{2}}}\overline{Z(\beta+iT)Z(\beta-iT)}$ , which is essential in studies of quantum chaos and quantum gravity [17, 19, 26]. The study of replica-nondiagonal saddle points of this and related quantities is the topic of the future work.

Below we consider the annealed correlators. The annealed correlation functions are computed by performing the average over the disorder in the normalization and in the nominator of (297) separately.

#### C.2.1 Single-replica correlators

If the fields all belong to the same one replica of the theory initially, the correlator is written

$$ \langle\psi_{i_{1}}(\tau_{1})\dots\psi_{i_{k}}(\tau_{k})\rangle_{\text{annealed}}=\frac{1}{\overline{Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;0)}}\frac{1}{k!}\left.\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta_{i_{1}}(\tau_{1})}\dots\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta_{i_{k}}(\tau_{k})}\overline{Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;\eta)}\right|_{\eta=0}\,. $$

The integral over the disorder is a straightforward Gaussian integral in both nominator and denominator and can be taken right away. The single-replica annealed correlators do not have any replica structure.

In terms of the bilocal fields $G$ , $\Sigma$ the annealed two-point function is written as

$$ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\langle\psi_{i}(\tau_{1})\psi_{i}(\tau_{2})\rangle_{\text{annealed}}=\frac{\int DGD\Sigma\ \mathrm{e}^{-NS[G,\Sigma]}G(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})}{\int DGD\Sigma\ \mathrm{e}^{-NS[G,\Sigma]}}\,. $$

#### C.2.2 Replica-offdiagonal correlators

Finally, one can consider the replica-offdiagonal annealed correlators of the form

$$ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\langle\psi_{i}^{\alpha}(\tau_{1})\psi^{\beta}_{i}(\tau_{2})\rangle_{\text{annealed}}=\frac{1}{2!N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\overline{Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;0)^{2}}}\left.\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta^{\alpha}_{i}(\tau_{1})}\frac{\delta}{\delta\eta^{\beta}_{i}(\tau_{2})}\overline{Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;\eta^{\alpha})Z_{{\bf j}}(\beta;\eta^{\beta})}\right|_{\eta=0}\,. $$

#### Factorization.

Note that this correlator does not factorize into product of one-point functions due to the fact that disorder averaging introduces interaction between replicas. However, the fermionic path integral still factorizes at finite $N$ . Taking the derivatives in the right hand side of (316), one obtains under the averaging line the product of two copies of

$$ \int D\psi\ \mathrm{e}^{-S_{\text{SYK}}[{\bf j},\psi]}\,. $$

This is zero at finite $N$ due to parity, and therefore also nullifies the correlator (316).

#### Bilocal field representation and $1/N$ -expansion.

In terms of the bilocal replica fields, the correlator (316) reads

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\langle\psi_{i}^{\alpha}(\tau_{1})\psi^{\beta}_{i}(\tau_{2})\rangle_{\text{annealed}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{\overline{Z(\beta)^{2}}}\mathfrak{G}_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};N,2) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{\int\prod_{\gamma,\delta=1}^{2}DG_{\gamma\delta}D\Sigma_{\gamma\delta}\ \mathrm{e}^{-NS[G_{\gamma\delta},\Sigma_{\gamma\delta}]}G_{\alpha\beta}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})}{\int\prod_{\gamma,\delta=1}^{2}DG_{\gamma\delta}D\Sigma_{\gamma\delta}\ \mathrm{e}^{-NS[G_{\gamma\delta},\Sigma_{\gamma\delta}]}}\,, $$

where $M=2$ . Note that there is a normalization factor, unlike the quenched case. This correlator requires two replicas, and can detect replica-nondiagonal saddle points, obtained in sections 3 and 4. We have shown that those saddle points are suppressed at large $N$ , thus their effect can only appear at finite $N$ .

However, at finite $N$ the factorization of the fermionic path integral dictates that (316) exactly should be zero. But here one can repeat the same arguments as in the disorder case in the end of sec.C.1.2. We can also expect that at finite $N$ the replica-nondiagonal saddle points may give a nonperturbatively small contribution to annealed $4$ - and higher-point nondiagonal correlators.

# Excitation spectra of quantum matter without quasiparticles I: Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev models

**Authors:** Maria Tikhanovskaya Affiliation: Department of Physics, Harvard University, Cambridge MA, 02138, USA Haoyu Guo Affiliation: Department of Physics, Harvard University, Cambridge MA, 02138, USA Subir Sachdev Affiliation: Department of Physics, Harvard University, Cambridge MA, 02138, USA Grigory Tarnopolsky Affiliation: Department of Physics, Harvard University, Cambridge MA, 02138, USA

## Abstract

We study the low frequency spectra of complex Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) models at general densities. The analysis applies also to SU( $M$ ) magnets with random exchange at large $M$ . The spectral densities are computed by numerical analysis of the saddle point equations on the real frequency ( $\omega$ ) axis at zero temperature ( $T$ ). The asymptotic low $\omega$ behaviors are found to be in excellent agreement with the scaling dimensions of irrelevant operators which perturb the conformally invariant critical states. Of possible experimental interest is our computation of the universal spin spectral weight of the SU( $M$ ) magnets at low $\omega$ and $T$ : this includes a contribution from the time reparameterization mode, which is the boundary graviton of the holographic dual. This analysis is extended to a random $t$ - $J$ model in a companion paper.

#### Contents

- I Introduction

- II Conformal solutions for the SYK models

- III Conformal perturbations

- IV Kitaev-Suh resonance theory IV.1 Linear order correction IV.2 Nonlinear order corrections IV.3 Finite Temperature Generalization

- V Spectral densities

- VI Random Quantum Rotor model

- VII Numerical results for spinon spectra

- VIII Conclusions

- A Free energy from conformal perturbations

- B Large $q$ two point function in the fermionic SYK model

- C Two point function for $q=2$ in the fermionic SYK model

- D Finite Temperature Generalization for Spectral Densities

- E Zero temperature numerics for the Bosonic/Fermionic SYK and the Random Rotor models

- References

## I Introduction

There has been much recent interest in solvable models [1, 2, 3] in the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) class as descriptions of compressible quantum many body systems without quasiparticle excitations. These are models with random and all-to-all interactions, and their low energy limit has the structure of 0+1 dimensional conformal field theory [4]. Instead of quasiparticles, there are infinite towers of primary operators [5, 6, 7, 8], all but a few of which have irrational scaling dimensions and these describe the long time dynamics of all local observables. We will examine a number of models of bosons and/or fermions in this paper, and the boson or fermion, $a=\mathfrak{b},f$ , has a zero temperature ( $T=0$ ) spectral density as a function of frequency, $\omega$ , of the form (for the case with $q=4$ -particle terms in the Hamiltonian)

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{a}(\omega)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{g_{a+}(\omega)}{\sqrt{\omega}},\quad\omega>0\\
\displaystyle\frac{g_{a-}(-\omega)}{\sqrt{-\omega}},\quad\omega<0\end{cases}\,. $$

Here $g_{a\pm}(\omega\rightarrow 0)=$ constant, and the main purpose of the present article is to describe the small $\omega$ expansions of $g_{a\pm}(\omega)$ for a number of models of physical interest. These expansions depend upon the scaling dimensions and operator product expansions of the irrelevant primary operators, and are also constrained by Luttinger-like theorems [9, 10, 11] and an emergent time reparameterization symmetry [6, 7]. We will compare conformal theory predictions with accurate numerical solutions of the SYK equations carried out directly on the real $\omega$ axis at $T=0$ (as in the original paper of Ref. [1]), and find excellent agreement.

A related analysis has been carried out by Maldacena and Stanford [6]. They examined the particle-hole symmetric Majorana SYK model, using numerical solutions of the SYK equations in imaginary time. All of our numerical analysis will be carried out in real time, using real frequency spectral functions: we will show that this allows higher precision, and enables us to identify various subleading and non-linear corrections. We also examine fermionic and bosonic models without particle-hole symmetry—the scaling dimensions for the particle-hole asymmetric fermionic models were obtained in Ref. [11].

Our results will also apply to the random quantum magnets with SU( $M$ ) symmetry which were studied in Ref. [1] in the limit of large $M$ . Such models are of interest to condensed matter physics because of their ‘Mottness’: they have constraints associated with strong on-site interactions, in contrast to the infinite-range interactions of the SYK models. For these magnets, we compute the dynamic local spin susceptibility $\chi_{L}(\omega)$ . This quantity is potentially of experimental interest as a description of a quantum critical point in a disordered magnetic system studied by neutron scattering [12, 13, 14, 15, 16]. The time reparameterization mode is the leading irrelevant operator determining the frequency dependence of $\chi_{L}$ , and we find

$$ \displaystyle\mbox{Im}\chi_{L}(\omega)\sim\tanh\left(\frac{\omega}{2T}\right)\left[1-\mathcal{C}\gamma\,\omega\tanh\left(\frac{\omega}{2T}\right)-\ldots\right]\,, $$

where the specific heat per spin component $=\gamma T$ , and $\mathcal{C}$ is a dimensionless number which is specified in (113) and (114) for our models. The leading term in (2) has been obtained earlier [4]. We obtain here the term proportional to $\mathcal{C}$ : this is the contribution of the time reparameterization mode i.e. the boundary graviton in the holographic dual. Notice that this term has a prefactor of $\omega$ without a corresponding factor of $1/T$ : this indicates the violation of scaling induced by an irrelevant operator. We show a plot of $\mbox{Im}\chi_{L}$ in Fig. 1; it is curious that this resembles observations in Refs. [13, 14], and it would be worthwhile to investigate this further, especially in systems with greater randomness.

*Figure 1: Plot of the local dynamic spin susceptibility. The blue solid line is obtained from numerical solution of the Schwinger-Dyson equations (16) for $T/J=0.1$ . The black dashed line is analytical result in (2) for $\mathcal{C}\gamma T\simeq 0.05$ with three higher order terms in (3) included with their $T=0$ expressions.*

Similar spectra should also apply to anomalous density fluctuations in the model of Ref. [17], and density fluctuations have been investigated in momentum-resolved electron energy-loss spectroscopy (M-EELS) [18, 19] but for $\omega\gg T$ .

In the limit of $T\rightarrow 0$ , (2) predicts a discontinous spectral density at zero frequency. We have computed higher order terms at $T=0$ for the particle-hole symmetric case (see Eq. (111))

$$ \mbox{Im}\chi_{L}(\omega)\sim\mbox{sgn}(\omega)\Bigl[1-\mathcal{C}\gamma|\omega|-\frac{7}{16}(\mathcal{C}\gamma)^{2}|\omega|^{2}-\mathcal{C}^{\prime}|\omega|^{2.77354\ldots}+\frac{37}{48}(\mathcal{C}\gamma)^{3}|\omega|^{3}-\ldots\Bigr]\,, $$

where the $|\omega|^{2}$ and $|\omega|^{3}$ terms are non-linear corrections from the time reparameterization mode, and $\mathcal{C}^{\prime}$ mode is a linear contribution of a second irrelevant operator with scaling dimension $h=3.77354\ldots$ . The $T>0$ form of the $\mathcal{C}^{\prime}$ term can be deduced from imaginary part of (187).

We have attempted to write this paper in a self-contained manner for condensed matter physicists. We will begin in Section II by defining the models of interest, and recalling the leading conformally invariant results. A diagrammatic analysis of the conformal perturbation theory is presented in Section III, where we obtain the scaling dimensions of all primary operators, and identify the operators associated with time reparameterization and an emergent U(1) gauge invariance. Section IV employs an alternative functional approach of Kitaev and Suh [7] which allows efficient treatment of particle-hole asymmetry, non-linear corrections and non-zero temperatures. Section V transforms our results from imaginary time to the spectral densities on the real frequency axis. Section VI extends our analysis to models of bosonic random rotors, which has appeared in some recent studies of quantum phase transitions. Finally, our main numerical results are presented in Section VII, where we compare numerical solutions of the SYK equations on the real frequency axis with the predictions of the conformal perturbation analysis.

The formalism developed in this paper for the SYK models will be applied to the $t$ - $J$ in a companion paper [20]. We will dope the large $M$ SU( $M$ ) insulating quantum magnets described in the present paper by mobile charge carriers. The resulting theory of fractionalized particles, the spinons and holons, is described [21] by a set of Schwinger-Dyson equations similar to those presented in Section II. The companion paper [20] presents the conformal corrections to a variety of gauge-invariant observables, including the electron spectral functions and the optical conductivity.

## II Conformal solutions for the SYK models

We begin by recalling the less-familiar models considered originally in Ref. [1], as these will connect directly to the $t$ - $J$ models considered in the companion paper [20]. These are SU( $M$ ) spin models with Hamiltonian

$$ H_{J}=\sum_{\left\langle ij\right\rangle,\alpha\beta}J_{ij}\left(S_{i\alpha\beta}S_{j\beta\alpha}-\frac{1}{M}S_{i\alpha\alpha}S_{j\beta\beta}\right). $$

Here $\alpha=1\ldots M$ is a SU( $M$ ) spin index, $S_{i\alpha\beta}=S_{i\beta\alpha}^{\dagger}$ is the spin operator on site $i$ , and the $1/M$ term (which will be dropped in large $M$ limit) is added to ensure it transform in the adjoint of SU $(M)$ . Here, we have chosen [4] to place the sites $i$ on a high-dimensional lattice with co-ordination number $z$ , and the $J_{ij}$ are nearest-neighbor exchange interactions and Gaussian random variables with

$$ \overline{J_{ij}}=0,\quad\overline{J_{ij}^{2}}=\frac{J^{2}}{Mz} $$

We will examine the model $H_{J}$ in the limit of large $z$ , followed by large $M$ . Alternatively, we can consider the model on a $N$ -site cluster, with all-to-all random exchange interactions; this was the model considered in Ref. [1], and the large $N$ limit leads to the same saddle-point equations as the large $z$ limit. However, the large $z$ limit allows us to consider transport properties of electrons in a lattice [4, 22] using a $t$ - $J$ model, which we will described in paper II.

The properties of the SU( $M$ ) spin models depend upon the representation of SU( $M$ ) realized by the states on each site, $i$ . The most common choices correspond to the formulations in terms of fermionic and bosonic spinons. The fermionic spinon case corresponds to the representation with a single column of boxes in the SU( $M$ ) Young tableaux, with the spin operator

$$ \displaystyle S_{i\alpha\beta} \displaystyle= \displaystyle f_{i\alpha}^{\dagger}f_{i\beta}. $$

expressed in terms of fermionic spinons $f_{i\alpha}$ . This induces a U(1) gauge symmetry

$$ f_{i\alpha}(\tau)\to f_{i\alpha}(\tau)e^{i\phi_{i}(\tau)},\quad $$

The physical Hilbert space must be U(1) gauge-symmetric, which implies that the gauge charge is conserved, and we consider the representation

$$ \sum_{\alpha}f_{i\alpha}^{\dagger}f_{i\alpha}=\kappa M, $$

with $\kappa M$ boxes in the Young tableaux. We will take the large $M$ limit at fixed $\kappa$ .

Similarly, the bosonic spinon case corresponds to a different SU( $M$ ) representation with a Young tableaux of a single row of boxes, and the spin operator

$$ \displaystyle S_{i\alpha\beta} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathfrak{b}_{i\alpha}^{\dagger}\mathfrak{b}_{i\beta}, $$

with the U(1) gauge charge constraint

$$ \sum_{\alpha}\mathfrak{b}^{\dagger}_{i\alpha}\mathfrak{b}_{i\alpha}=\kappa M\,. $$

The fermionic spinon representation defined by (6) and (8) and the bosonic spinon representation defined by (9) and (10) are the same only for $\kappa M=1$ .

Along with the SU( $M$ ) spin models recalled above, our results apply also to the complex SYK model (with a $q=4$ fermion Hamiltonian)

$$ H_{\textrm{SYK}}=\frac{1}{2N^{3/2}}\sum_{i,j,k,\ell=1}^{N}J_{ij;k\ell}f_{i}^{\dagger}f_{j}^{\dagger}f_{k}f_{\ell}-\mu_{f}\sum_{i}f_{i}^{\dagger}f_{i} $$

where $J_{ij;k\ell}$ are independent random numbers with $\overline{|J_{ij;k\ell}|^{2}}=J^{2}$ . The advantage of this model is that only a single large $N$ limit is required, and there is no analog of the subsequent large $M$ limit required for the models above. But, as we discussed in Section I, this simplicity comes at a cost: we loose the Mottness that is present in the spin (and $t$ - $J$ ) models, and is important for condensed matter applications. The analog of the fermion constraint in (8) is now

$$ \langle f_{i}^{\dagger}f_{i}\rangle=\kappa\,, $$

with no sum over $i$ . Analogously to the fermionic SYK model we can define bosonic SYK model as

$$ H_{\textrm{SYK}}=\frac{1}{2N^{3/2}}\sum_{i,j,k,\ell=1}^{N}J_{ij;k\ell}\mathfrak{b}_{i}^{\dagger}\mathfrak{b}_{j}^{\dagger}\mathfrak{b}_{k}\mathfrak{b}_{\ell}-\mu_{\mathfrak{b}}\sum_{i}\mathfrak{b}_{i}^{\dagger}\mathfrak{b}_{i}\,, $$

along with the constraint

$$ \langle\mathfrak{b}_{i}^{\dagger}\mathfrak{b}_{i}\rangle=\kappa\,. $$

We remark that the bosonic models defined above have $\mathfrak{b}^{{\dagger}}\partial_{\tau}\mathfrak{b}$ kinetic term in the Lagrangian formalism.

All of the above models have a common set of saddle point equations, which we now describe. We introduce two-point Green’s function in imaginary time, $\tau$ , at a finite temperature $T$ :

$$ \displaystyle G_{f}(\tau)=-\langle\textrm{T}_{\tau}\big(f(\tau)f^{{\dagger}}(0)\big)\rangle\,,\quad G_{b}(\tau)=-\langle\textrm{T}_{\tau}\big(\mathfrak{b}(\tau)\mathfrak{b}^{{\dagger}}(0)\big)\rangle\,. $$

In both cases the large $N$ Dyson-Schwinger equations look identical and read for $\tau\in(0,\beta)$

$$ \displaystyle G_{a}(i\omega_{n})=\frac{1}{i\omega_{n}+\mu_{a}-\Sigma_{a}(i\omega_{n})},\quad\Sigma_{a}(\tau)=J^{2}G_{a}(\tau)^{q/2}G_{a}(\beta-\tau)^{q/2-1}\,, $$

where the index $a=f,\mathfrak{b}$ denotes fermions or bosons, $\beta=1/T$ is the inverse temperature, $\mu_{a}$ is the chemical potential and we assume that $q$ is even integer. The models described above have $q=4$ , but we will also present some results for general $q$ . For the fermionic case the Matsubara frequencies is $\omega_{n}=\frac{2\pi}{\beta}(n+\frac{1}{2})$ and for the bosonic $\omega_{n}=\frac{2\pi}{\beta}n$ . The two-point Green’s function satisfies the KMS (Kubo-Martin-Schwinger) conditions $G_{a}(\tau)=\zeta_{a}G_{a}(\beta+\tau)$ , where $\zeta_{\mathfrak{b}}=1$ and $\zeta_{f}=-1$ .

It is well-known that the equations (16) admit conformal solution in the IR region, where $1/J\ll\tau\ll\beta-1/J$

$$ \displaystyle G^{c}_{a}(\tau)=-b_{a}^{\Delta}\left(\frac{\beta J}{\pi}\sin\frac{\pi\tau}{\beta}\right)^{-2\Delta}e^{2\pi\mathscr{E}_{a}(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\tau}{\beta})}\,, \displaystyle\Sigma^{c}_{a}(\tau)=-J^{2}b_{a}^{1-\Delta}\left(\frac{\beta J}{\pi}\sin\frac{\pi\tau}{\beta}\right)^{-2(1-\Delta)}e^{2\pi\mathscr{E}_{a}(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\tau}{\beta})}\,, $$

where $\Delta=1/q$ , $\mathscr{E}_{a}$ is the asymmetry parameter which implicitly depends on $\mu$ , and the dimensionless constant prefactor $b_{a}$ is

$$ \displaystyle b_{f}=\frac{(1-2\Delta)\sin 2\pi\Delta}{4\pi\cos(\pi(\Delta+i\mathscr{E}_{f}))\cos(\pi(\Delta-i\mathscr{E}_{f}))}\,,\quad b_{\mathfrak{b}}=\frac{(1-2\Delta)\sin 2\pi\Delta}{4\pi\sin(\pi(\Delta+i\mathscr{E}_{\mathfrak{b}}))\sin(\pi(\Delta-i\mathscr{E}_{\mathfrak{b}}))}\,. $$

When we work in frequency space, it turns out to be convenient to use the asymmetry angles $\theta_{a}$ related to $\mathscr{E}_{a}$ by

$$ \displaystyle e^{2\pi\mathscr{E}_{a}}=\zeta_{a}\frac{\sin(\theta_{a}+\pi\Delta)}{\sin(\theta_{a}-\pi\Delta)},\quad e^{-2i\theta_{f}}=\frac{\cos(\pi(\Delta+i\mathscr{E}_{f}))}{\cos(\pi(\Delta-i\mathscr{E}_{f}))}\,,\quad e^{-2i\theta_{\mathfrak{b}}}=-\frac{\sin(\pi(\Delta+i\mathscr{E}_{\mathfrak{b}}))}{\sin(\pi(\Delta-i\mathscr{E}_{\mathfrak{b}}))}\,, $$

therefore we can find

$$ \displaystyle b_{a}=\zeta_{a}\frac{(1-2\Delta)}{\pi}\frac{\sin(\theta_{a}+\pi\Delta)\sin(\theta_{a}-\pi\Delta)}{\sin 2\pi\Delta}\,. $$

Notice that $\mathscr{E}_{\mathfrak{b}}=0$ for $\theta_{\mathfrak{b}}=\pi/2$ and $\mathscr{E}_{f}=0$ for $\theta_{f}=0$ . Also $\pi\Delta<\theta_{\mathfrak{b}}<\pi/2$ and $-\pi\Delta<\theta_{f}<\pi\Delta$ .

Below, we will study the structure of the conformal corrections to the large $z$ and large $M$ saddle point of $H_{J}$ in (4), and the large $N$ saddle-point of $H_{\rm SYK}$ in (11). The Schwinger-Dyson equations at the saddle point are identical in the two models, so the conformal corrections will also be the same. However, once we go beyond the saddle point, and examine four-point correlators, there will be differences between the two models. We will not address these differences here.

## III Conformal perturbations

In this section we describe a useful view point on the SYK models as a conformal field theory (CFT) perturbed by infinite set of irrelevant operators. Although this approach is not rigorous and has caveats, which we mention below, it clarifies understanding of some results and can correctly predict $1/(\beta J)$ and $1/(\beta J)^{2}$ corrections to the free energy (see Appendix A). We will turn to a more complete approach to similar results in Section IV.

For simplicity, in this section we consider only the fermionic SYK model (11) with zero chemical potential $\mu=0$ , as the generalization to $\mu\neq 0$ is described in Section IV. It was shown in Refs. [23, 24, 25] that this model has an infinite set of bilinear primary operators $O_{h}^{\textrm{A}}(\tau)$ and $O_{h}^{\textrm{S}}(\tau)$ , which can be schematically represented as $O_{h_{n}}^{\textrm{A}}=f^{{\dagger}}_{i}\partial_{\tau}^{2n+1}f_{i}$ and $O_{h_{n}}^{\textrm{S}}=f^{{\dagger}}_{i}\partial_{\tau}^{2n}f_{i}$ for $n=0,1,2,\dots$ . To compute the scaling dimensions of the operators $O_{h}^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}(\tau)$ we consider three point functions

$$ v^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}_{h}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2},\tau_{0})=\langle f(\tau_{1})f^{\dagger}(\tau_{2})O^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}_{h}(\tau_{0})\rangle\,. $$

Then we can derive the Dyson-Schwinger equations for the three point functions in the IR region, and we can drop the bare terms to obtain [23]

$$ v^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}_{h}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2},\tau_{0})=\int d\tau_{3}d\tau_{4}K_{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};\tau_{3},\tau_{4})v^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}_{h}(\tau_{3},\tau_{4},\tau_{0})\,, $$

where the kernels $K_{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}$ are

$$ K_{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};\tau_{3},\tau_{4})=-\Big(\frac{q}{2}\pm\Big(\frac{q}{2}-1\Big)\Big)J^{2}G^{c}(\tau_{13})G^{c}(\tau_{24})G^{c}(\tau_{34})^{q-2}\,. $$

Diagramatically the equations (22) are represented in Fig.2.

*Figure 2: Diagrammatic representation of the Dyson-Schwinger equations (22), after dropping the bare terms. The internal loop has $q-2$ powers of $G^{c}$ (this diagram is for $q=6$ ).*

Emergent conformal symmetry in the IR region fixes the functional form of the three-point functions up to the structure constants $c_{h}^{\textrm{A}}$ and $c_{h}^{\textrm{S}}$

$$ v^{\textrm{A}}_{h}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2},\tau_{0})=\frac{c_{h}^{\textrm{A}}b^{\Delta}\,\textrm{sgn}(\tau_{12})}{|J\tau_{12}|^{2\Delta-h}|J\tau_{10}|^{h}|J\tau_{20}|^{h}},\quad v^{\textrm{S}}_{h}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2},\tau_{0})=\frac{c_{h}^{\textrm{S}}b^{\Delta}\,\textrm{sgn}(\tau_{10})\textrm{sgn}(\tau_{20})}{|J\tau_{12}|^{2\Delta-h}|J\tau_{10}|^{h}|J\tau_{20}|^{h}}\,. $$

It can be shown that for arbitrary $h$ the three-point functions $v^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}_{h}$ satisfy the equation [6, 7, 24, 25]

$$ \int d\tau_{3}d\tau_{4}K_{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};\tau_{3},\tau_{4})v^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}_{h}(\tau_{3},\tau_{4},\tau_{0})=k_{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}(h)v^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}_{h}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2},\tau_{0})\,, $$

where $k_{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}(h)$ are given by the formulas

$$ \displaystyle k_{\textrm{A}}(h)=\frac{\Gamma(2\Delta-h)\Gamma(2\Delta+h-1)}{\Gamma(2\Delta-2)\Gamma(2\Delta+1)}\left(1-\frac{\sin(\pi h)}{\sin(2\pi\Delta)}\right)\,, \displaystyle k_{\textrm{S}}(h)=\frac{\Gamma(2\Delta-h)\Gamma(2\Delta+h-1)}{\Gamma(2\Delta-1)\Gamma(2\Delta)}\left(1+\frac{\sin(\pi h)}{\sin(2\pi\Delta)}\right)\,. $$

This formula can be verified by taking the limit $|\tau_{0}|\rightarrow\infty$ in (25) and then evaluating the integrals over $\tau_{3,4}$ . Therefore comparing (25) with (22), we have to set

$$ k_{\textrm{A}}(h)=1\quad,\quad k_{\textrm{S}}(h)=1\,, $$

and these equations define the anomalous scaling dimensions of the operators $O_{h}^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}(\tau)$ .

The SYK model can be viewed as some conformal field theory perturbed by this infinite set of irrelevant primary operators. In the case of zero chemical potential $\mu=0$ there is an exact particle-hole symmetry and thus only $O_{h}^{\textrm{A}}$ operators can appear in the action. This situation exactly coincides with the case of the Majorana SYK model, where instead of complex fermions $f_{i}$ we have Majorana fermions $\chi_{i}$ . Therefore in what follows we omit letter “A” for brevity and write for the effective action of the Majorana SYK model

$$ \displaystyle S_{\textrm{SYK}}=S_{\textrm{CFT}}+\sum_{h}g_{h}\int_{0}^{\beta}d\tau O_{h}(\tau)\,, $$

where $O_{h}$ have anomalous dimensions $h=h_{0},h_{1},h_{2},h_{3},\dots$ and $h_{0}=2$ , $h_{1}\simeq 3.77,h_{2}\simeq 5.68$ , etc, which are found from the equation $k_{\textrm{A}}(h)=1$ . (A notational aside: we will often use the subscript $i$ to represent the subscript $h_{i}$ e.g. $g_{h_{2}}\equiv g_{2}$ .)

The expression for the full two point function reads

$$ \displaystyle G(\tau_{12})=-\frac{1}{Z}\int D\chi\frac{1}{N}\chi_{i}(\tau_{1})\chi_{i}(\tau_{2})e^{-S_{\textrm{SYK}}}\,, $$

therefore using conformal perturbation theory we find

$$ \displaystyle G(\tau_{12})= \displaystyle G^{c}(\tau_{12})+\sum_{h}g_{h}\int d\tau_{3}\frac{1}{N}\langle\chi_{i}(\tau_{1})\chi_{i}(\tau_{2})O_{h}(\tau_{3})\rangle \displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{h,h^{\prime}}g_{h}g_{h^{\prime}}\int d\tau_{3}d\tau_{4}\frac{1}{N}\langle\chi_{i}(\tau_{1})\chi_{i}(\tau_{2})O_{h}(\tau_{3})O_{h^{\prime}}(\tau_{4})\rangle+\dots\,, $$

where we used that $G^{c}(\tau_{12})=-\frac{1}{N}\langle\chi_{i}(\tau_{1})\chi_{i}(\tau_{2})\rangle$ and averaging of the correlation functions is implicitly performed with $S_{\textrm{CFT}}$ action and involves only connected diagrams. The higher correlation functions are fixed by conformal invariance up to the structure constants $c_{h}$ and $c_{h_{1}h_{2}h_{3}}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{N}\langle\chi_{i}(\tau_{1})\chi_{i}(\tau_{2})O_{h}(\tau_{3})\rangle=\frac{c_{h}b^{\Delta}\,\textrm{sgn}(\tau_{12})}{|J\tau_{12}|^{2\Delta-h}|J\tau_{13}|^{h}|J\tau_{23}|^{h}}\,, \displaystyle\frac{1}{N}\langle\chi_{i}(\tau_{1})\chi_{i}(\tau_{2})O_{h_{1}}(\tau_{3})O_{h_{2}}(\tau_{4})\rangle=\sum_{h}\frac{c_{h}c_{hh_{1}h_{2}}b^{\Delta}\textrm{sgn}(\tau_{12})|\tau_{14}|^{h_{12}}}{|J\tau_{12}|^{2\Delta}|J\tau_{34}|^{h_{1}+h_{2}}|\tau_{13}|^{h_{12}}}x^{h}\,_{2}F_{1}(h,h+h_{12},2h,x)\,, $$

where $h_{12}=h_{1}-h_{2}$ and $x=\frac{\tau_{12}\tau_{34}}{\tau_{13}\tau_{24}}$ . Alternatively they can be found from the Operator Product Expansion (OPE)

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{N}\chi_{i}(\tau_{1})\chi^{{\dagger}}_{i}(\tau_{2})=\frac{b^{\Delta}\,\textrm{sgn}(\tau_{12})}{|J\tau_{12}|^{2\Delta}}+\frac{1}{N}\sum_{h}\frac{c_{h}b^{\Delta}\,\textrm{sgn}(\tau_{12})}{|J\tau_{12}|^{2\Delta-h}}\mathcal{C}_{h}(\tau_{12},\partial_{2})O_{h}(\tau_{2})\,, \displaystyle O_{h_{1}}(\tau_{1})O_{h_{2}}(\tau_{2})=\frac{N\delta_{hh^{\prime}}}{|J\tau_{12}|^{2h}}+\sum_{h^{\prime\prime}}c_{h_{1}h_{2}h_{3}}|J\tau_{12}|^{h_{3}-h_{1}-h_{2}}\mathcal{C}_{123}(\tau_{12},\partial_{2})O_{h_{3}}(\tau_{2})\,, $$

where $b=\frac{1}{2\pi}(1-2\Delta)\tan(\pi\Delta)$ and the operators $\mathcal{C}_{h}$ and $\mathcal{C}_{123}$ generate all descendants and are determined by the functional form of the three-point functions. The structure constants $c_{h}$ are [6]

$$ \displaystyle c_{h}^{2}=\frac{1}{(q-1)b^{\Delta}}\cdot\frac{(h-1/2)}{\pi\tan(\pi h/2)}\frac{\Gamma(h)^{2}}{\Gamma(2h)}\cdot\frac{1}{k_{\textrm{A}}^{\prime}(h)}\,, $$

and $c_{hh^{\prime}h^{\prime\prime}}$ have much more complicated form and were computed in Refs. [26, 8]. The OPE formulas (32) should not include $h_{0}=2$ operator, since it was shown in [6] that this operator breaks conformal symmetry in the SYK model. Moreover we notice that $c_{h}$ is divergent for $h_{0}=2$ . Nevertheless let us assume that we deal with unbroken CFT and can include $O_{h_{0}}$ operator in the OPE formulas assuming limit $h_{0}\to 2$ 11 1 Perhaps this approach can be justified if the SYK model is considered as a limit of some conformal SYK model for which $h_{0}=2-\epsilon_{0}$ and $\epsilon_{0}\to 0$ , see [Gross:2017vhb] and Appendix H in [6]. .

For the first order correction to the two point function at zero temperature $\beta=\infty$ we find

$$ \displaystyle\delta G_{h}(\tau_{12}) \displaystyle=g_{h}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}d\tau_{3}\frac{c_{h}b^{\Delta}\,\textrm{sgn}(\tau_{12})}{|J\tau_{12}|^{2\Delta-h}|J\tau_{13}|^{h}|J\tau_{23}|^{h}}=-G^{c}(\tau_{12})\frac{\alpha_{h}}{|J\tau_{12}|^{h-1}}\,, $$

where $\alpha_{h}$ and $g_{h}$ are related as

$$ \displaystyle g_{h}^{2}=J^{2}(q-1)b^{\Delta}k_{\textrm{A}}^{\prime}(h)\frac{(h-1/2)}{\pi\tan(\pi h/2)}\frac{\Gamma(h)^{2}}{\Gamma(2h)}\alpha_{h}^{2}\,. $$

We notice that $g_{0}$ has to be divergent for $h_{0}=2$ in order for $\alpha_{0}$ to be finite. Also we remark that all $g_{h}\propto J$ are dimensionful couplings, whereas $\alpha_{h}$ are dimensionless constants. The analysis in Section IV establishes that $\alpha_{0}$ is indeed finite, and we will confirm this in our numerical results.

For the second order correction we find using (31)

$$ \displaystyle\delta^{2}G_{hh^{\prime}}(\tau_{12})=-\frac{1}{2}g_{h}g_{h^{\prime}}\int d\tau_{3}d\tau_{4}\frac{1}{N}\langle\chi_{i}(\tau_{1})\chi_{i}(\tau_{2})O_{h}(\tau_{3})O_{h^{\prime}}(\tau_{4})\rangle=-G^{c}(\tau_{12})\frac{a_{hh^{\prime}}\alpha_{h}\alpha_{h^{\prime}}}{2|J\tau_{12}|^{h+h^{\prime}-2}}\,, $$

where the coefficients $a_{hh^{\prime}}$ are functions of $h$ , $h^{\prime}$ and $\Delta$ and we will find some of them explicitly in the Section IV using resonance theory.

It is instructive to use these conformal perturbation methods to also compute the free energy. We describe this in Appendix A; one term is at variance with another discussion [28].

## IV Kitaev-Suh resonance theory

In this section, we will review the renormalization and resonance formalism developed in [7, 11, 22], and extend it to nonlinear order. The theory provides a framework for understanding the corrections due to physics at higher energy scales in SYK-type models.

To linear order, the corrected Green’s function in (30) $G(\tau)=-\langle\textrm{T}_{\tau}f(\tau)f^{\dagger}(0)\rangle$ can be written as

$$ G(\tau)=G^{c}(\tau)\left(1-\sum_{h}\frac{\alpha_{h}}{(\beta J)^{h-1}}\mathcal{F}_{h}(\tau/\beta)+\dots\right). $$

Here recall that $G^{c}(\tau)$ is the conformal Green’s function, $\beta$ is inverse temperature and $J$ denotes some UV energy scale, which is usually taken to be the SYK coupling. $\mathcal{F}_{h}$ is some universal scaling functions that will be computed later in (98). The sum runs over a set of discrete numbers $\{h_{i}\}$ that will be determined in Section IV.1. Although the resonance formalism is a direct consequence of Schwinger-Dyson equations, the structure of the corrections is consistent with the CFT interpretation of SYK-type model. The numbers $\{h_{i}\}$ can be interpreted as the scaling dimensions of primary operators $\{O_{h}\}$ in the SYK CFT that appears in the OPE of $f(\tau)f^{\dagger}(0)$ . The dimensionless coefficients $\alpha_{h}$ parameterize the deformation away from the SYK CFT, as in (28).

The exact values of $\alpha_{h}$ ’s require solving the full Schwinger-Dyson equations in the UV, and they are usually extracted from numerics.

In SYK-type models, operators $O_{0}^{\textrm{S}}$ (there may be several) of scaling dimension $h_{0}^{\textrm{S}}=1$ and $O_{0}^{\textrm{A}}$ of scaling dimension $h_{0}^{\textrm{A}}=2$ are special: they are the conserved charges of $U(1)$ and time-reparameterization symmetry respectively. These symmetries are emergent and spontaneously broken in the IR, but also explicitly broken by the deformation $\delta S$ which lives in the UV. Therefore $\delta S$ provides the effective action for the these pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone modes. For the time-reparameterization symmetry, this is the well-known Schwarzian action.

The resonance formalism was first developed in [7] for Majorana SYK, where the Green’s function is always antisymmetric in time and $\mathcal{F}_{h}$ is obtained for generic temperature. In [11], the formalism was extended to complex SYK model which has a $U(1)$ symmetry, and $\mathcal{F}_{h}$ is obtained at zero temperature for generic $U(1)$ charge. In [22], the theory was further extended to the $t$ - $J$ model, a couple system of both fermions and bosons, and the scaling function $\mathcal{F}_{h}$ was obtained for generic temperature and $U(1)$ charge. In all these previous works, the correction is only calculated for linear order in $\alpha_{h}$ , which only provides information about the spectral weight $\rho_{a}(\omega)$ around $\omega=0$ . In this paper, we will extend the formalism to arbitrary nonlinear order in $\alpha_{h}$ , which shows excellent agreement with large- $q$ expansion and numerics at finite $q$ : it can now extrapolate the spectral weight $\rho_{a}(\omega)$ up to finite $\omega/J$ .

### IV.1 Linear order correction

We summarize previous works on linear order resonance theory [7, 11, 22]. Our discussion will be based on the Schwinger-Dyson equation, abstractly written as

$$ G=G_{*}[\Sigma],\quad\Sigma=\Sigma_{*}[G]+\sigma. $$

Here $G$ and $\Sigma$ are regarded as bi-local fields and $G_{*}$ and $\Sigma_{*}$ are functionals that define the saddle point. $\sigma$ is a bi-local field referred as the UV source. The conformal solution $(G^{c},\Sigma^{c})$ is exact if $\sigma=0$ . In the bosonic and fermionic $\text{SYK}_{q}$ models, $G_{*}[\Sigma](\tau_{1},\tau_{2})=-(1/\Sigma)(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})$ (in the sense of functional inverse), and $\Sigma_{*}[G](\tau_{1},\tau_{2})=(-)^{\epsilon_{a}}J^{2}G(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})^{q/2}\left(-G(\tau_{2},\tau_{1})\right)^{q/2-1}$ , and $\sigma(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})=(\partial_{\tau_{1}}-\mu)\delta(\tau_{1}-\tau_{2})$ . $\sigma$ is referred as UV source because it contains high frequency Fourier components. We also note that the self-energy $\Sigma$ is shifted from the usual definition by $\sigma$ .

If we are interested in the IR physics $J^{-1}\ll|\tau|\lesssim\beta$ , the UV source $\sigma$ can be treated as small perturbation, the small parameter being the ratio between IR and UV scales $1/(\beta J)^{h-1}$ or $1/|J\tau|^{h-1}$ . To calculate the linear response, we expand the SD equations (38) around the conformal saddle point $(G^{c},\Sigma^{c})$ to linear order:

$$ G=G^{c}+\delta G,\quad\Sigma=\Sigma^{c}+\delta\Sigma. $$

and obtain

$$ \delta G=W_{\Sigma}\delta\Sigma,\quad\delta\Sigma=W_{G}\delta G+\sigma $$

where we defined $W_{\Sigma}$ and $W_{G}$ as

$$ W_{\Sigma}=\left.\frac{\delta G_{*}}{\delta\Sigma}\right|_{\Sigma^{c}},\qquad W_{G}=\left.\frac{\delta\Sigma_{*}}{\delta G}\right|_{G^{c}}. $$

Finally a simple analysis yields [11]:

$$ \delta G=(1-\underbrace{W_{\Sigma}W_{G}}_{K_{G}})^{-1}W_{\Sigma}\sigma\,,\quad\delta\Sigma=(1-\underbrace{W_{G}W_{\Sigma}}_{K_{\Sigma}})^{-1}\sigma\,. $$

Here we defined two kernels $K_{G}=W_{\Sigma}W_{G}$ and $K_{\Sigma}=W_{G}W_{\Sigma}$ . We remark that $K_{G}$ is exactly the one-rung diagrams that one needs to sum to compute the four-point functions [6, 7]. By construction the nonzero spectra of $K_{G}$ and $K_{\Sigma}$ are the same.

In what follows we are going to adopt a convenient notation used in Ref. [11] for writing functions which have discontinuity at $\tau=0$ and different behaviour for negative and positive $\tau$ . Namely, we write all functions as two component vectors, where the first component is for $\tau>0$ and the second one is for $\tau<0$ . We refer to this as a plus/minus basis. For example the conformal solution for the Green’s function $G^{c}_{a}(\tau)$ and self-energy $\Sigma^{c}_{a}(\tau)$ at zero temperature can be written as

$$ \displaystyle G^{c}_{a}(\tau) \displaystyle=-\begin{pmatrix}e^{\pi\mathscr{E}_{a}},\quad\tau>0\\
\zeta_{a}e^{-\pi\mathscr{E}_{a}},\;\tau<0\end{pmatrix}\frac{b_{a}^{\Delta}}{|J\tau|^{2\Delta}}\,,\quad\Sigma^{c}_{a}(\tau)=-\begin{pmatrix}e^{\pi\mathscr{E}_{a}},\quad\tau>0\\
\zeta_{a}e^{-\pi\mathscr{E}_{a}},\;\tau<0\end{pmatrix}\frac{J^{2}b_{a}^{1-\Delta}}{|J\tau|^{2(1-\Delta)}}\,, $$

where the constant $b_{a}$ is given in (20) and $\zeta_{\mathfrak{b}}=1$ and $\zeta_{f}=-1$ . In what follows we suppress index $a=f,\mathfrak{b}$ in various functions for brevity and only keep $\zeta$ factors where it’s needed.

To proceed in analysis, we notice that the conformal saddle point possesses ${\rm SL}(2,R)$ symmetry, and therefore we can break up (42) into irreducible representations of ${\rm SL}(2,R)$ labelled by $h$ , and a convenient basis for this purpose at zero temperature is

$$ \delta G(\tau)=\delta\vec{G}|J\tau|^{1-h}G^{c}(\tau),\quad\delta\Sigma(\tau)=\delta\vec{\Sigma}|J\tau|^{1-h}\Sigma^{c}(\tau),\quad\sigma(\tau)=\sum_{h}\vec{\sigma}_{h}|J\tau|^{1-h}\Sigma^{c}(\tau)u(\tau)\,, $$

where $\delta\vec{G}=(\delta G_{+},\delta G_{-})^{\textrm{T}}$ , $\delta\vec{\Sigma}=(\delta\Sigma_{+},\delta\Sigma_{-})^{\textrm{T}}$ and $\vec{\sigma}_{h}=(\sigma_{h+},\sigma_{h-})^{\textrm{T}}$ are all two components columns according to our new notations and the source $\sigma(\tau)$ is written in the IR region with the window function $u(\tau)$ and positive real numbers $h$ (for details about this representation of the soruce $\sigma$ see Ref. [7]). In this basis, $W_{\Sigma}$ , $W_{G}$ and $K_{G}$ , $K_{\Sigma}$ become $2\times 2$ dimensional matrices. So for the fermionic and bosonic $\text{SYK}_{q}$ models (16), we can find

$$ \delta\Sigma_{*}(\tau)|_{G^{c}}=\left(\frac{q}{2}\frac{\delta G(\tau)}{G^{c}(\tau)}+\Big(\frac{q}{2}-1\Big)\frac{\delta G(-\tau)}{G^{c}(-\tau)}\right)\Sigma^{c}(\tau) $$

and using the basis (44) we write it as

$$ \delta\Sigma_{*}(\tau)|_{G^{c}}=W_{G}\delta\vec{G}|J\tau|^{1-h}\Sigma^{c}(\tau)\,, $$

where $W_{G}$ becomes a $2\times 2$ matrix given by the formula

$$ W_{G}=\begin{pmatrix}q/2&q/2-1\\
q/2-1&q/2\end{pmatrix}. $$

To find expression for the operator $W_{\Sigma}$ we are going to use the Fourier transform written in our convenient plus/minus basis

$$ \mathop{\text{\large$\int$}}\nolimits\begin{pmatrix}a_{+}|\tau|^{-\alpha},\quad\tau>0\\
a_{-}|\tau|^{-\alpha},\quad\tau<0\end{pmatrix}e^{i\omega\tau}d\tau=\begin{pmatrix}a^{\prime}_{+}|\omega|^{\alpha-1},\quad\omega>0\\
a^{\prime}_{-}|\omega|^{\alpha-1},\quad\omega<0\end{pmatrix}\,,\quad\begin{pmatrix}a_{+}^{\prime}\\
a_{-}^{\prime}\end{pmatrix}=M(\alpha)\begin{pmatrix}a_{+}\\
a_{-}\end{pmatrix}\,, $$

where the $2\times 2$ matrix $M(\alpha)$ has the form

$$ M(\alpha)=\Gamma(1-\alpha)\begin{pmatrix}i^{1-\alpha}&i^{\alpha-1}\\
i^{\alpha-1}&i^{1-\alpha}\end{pmatrix}\,,\quad M(\alpha)^{-1}=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha)}{2\pi}\begin{pmatrix}i^{-\alpha}&i^{\alpha}\\
i^{\alpha}&i^{-\alpha}\end{pmatrix}\,. $$

In the Fourier space the basis (44) takes the form

$$ \displaystyle\delta G(i\omega)=F(h)\delta\vec{G}|\omega/J|^{h-1}G^{c}(i\omega),\quad\delta\Sigma(i\omega)=\Phi(h)\delta\vec{\Sigma}|\omega/J|^{h-1}\Sigma^{c}(i\omega)\,, $$

where the matrices $F(h)$ and $\Phi(h)$ are

$$ \displaystyle F(h) \displaystyle=-i\sqrt{\frac{\Gamma(2\Delta)}{\Gamma(2-2\Delta)}}b^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}e^{i\theta}&0\\
0&-e^{-i\theta}\\
\end{array}\right)M(2\Delta-1+h)\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}e^{\pi\mathscr{E}}&0\\
0&\zeta e^{-\pi\mathscr{E}}\\
\end{array}\right)\,, \displaystyle\Phi(h) \displaystyle=-i\sqrt{\frac{\Gamma(2-2\Delta)}{\Gamma(2\Delta)}}b^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}e^{-i\theta}&0\\
0&-e^{i\theta}\\
\end{array}\right)M(1-2\Delta+h)\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}e^{\pi\mathscr{E}}&0\\
0&\zeta e^{-\pi\mathscr{E}}\\
\end{array}\right)\,. $$

and we used formulas for $G^{c}(i\omega)$ and $\Sigma^{c}(i\omega)$ in the Fourier space at zero temperature:

$$ \displaystyle G^{c}(i\omega) \displaystyle=-\frac{iC}{J}\begin{pmatrix}e^{-i\theta}\\
-e^{i\theta}\end{pmatrix}|\omega/J|^{2\Delta-1}\,,\quad\Sigma^{c}(i\omega)=-\frac{iJ}{C}\begin{pmatrix}e^{i\theta}\\
-e^{-i\theta}\end{pmatrix}|\omega/J|^{1-2\Delta}\,, $$

where we defined $C\equiv\sqrt{\Gamma(2-2\Delta)/\Gamma(2\Delta)}b^{\Delta-\frac{1}{2}}$ . Notice that there are no $\zeta$ factors in (59). The operator $W_{\Sigma}$ connects linear corrections $\delta\Sigma$ and $\delta G$ as $\delta G=W_{\Sigma}\delta\Sigma$ and has a simple form in the Fourier space

$$ \displaystyle\delta G_{*}(i\omega)|_{\Sigma^{c}}=G^{c}(i\omega)^{2}\delta\Sigma(i\omega)\,. $$

Thus using (50) and $G^{c}(i\omega)\Sigma^{c}(i\omega)=-1$ we find

$$ \displaystyle F(h)\delta\vec{G}=-\Phi(h)\delta\vec{\Sigma}\, $$

and therefore $W_{\Sigma}$ acts on $\delta\vec{\Sigma}$ as a matrix $W_{\Sigma}(h)=-F(h)^{-1}\Phi(h)$ and is given by the formula [11]:

$$ W_{\Sigma}(h)=\frac{\Gamma(2\Delta-1+h)\Gamma(2\Delta-h)}{\Gamma(2\Delta)\Gamma(2\Delta-1)\sin(2\pi\Delta)}\begin{pmatrix}\sin(\pi h+2\theta)&-\sin(2\pi\Delta)+\sin(2\theta)\\
-\sin(2\pi\Delta)-\sin(2\theta)&\sin(\pi h-2\theta)\end{pmatrix}\,. $$

We notice that the matrix $W_{\Sigma}(h)$ has the same form for bosonic and fermionic SYK models and the only difference is the range of asymmetry angle $\theta$ in these two cases. The matrix $K_{G}(h)$ is a product of two matrices $W_{\Sigma}(h)$ and $W_{G}$ , so $K_{G}(h)=W_{\Sigma}(h)W_{G}$ . Therefore (42) reads

$$ \delta G=\frac{1}{1-K_{G}(h)}W_{\Sigma}(h)\sigma. $$

For generic $h$ , $1-K_{G}(h)$ is non-singular and therefore the response $\delta G$ is negligible at IR scales. We need to remember that a physical source $\sigma$ is supported only in the UV, and we expect a non-singular response $\delta G$ is also constrained in the UV region. To get an IR response, $1-K_{G}(h)$ should be singular, so the possible $h$ ’s that appear in (37) is selected by the condition

$$ \det(1-K_{G}(h))=0\,. $$

For the particle-hole symmetric case, $\mu=0$ , this equation is equivalent to $k_{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}(h)=1$ where $k_{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}(h)$ are defined in (26).

For the resonant values of $h=h_{*}$ , the apparent singluarity in (63) is regulated by the window function $u(\tau)$ which restricts $\sigma$ to be supported only on UV scales. Following [7, 11] we obtain

$$ \delta G(\tau)=\sum_{h=h_{*}}\frac{1}{K_{G}^{\prime}(h)}W_{\Sigma}(h)\vec{\sigma}_{h}|J\tau|^{1-h}G^{c}(\tau)\,, $$

where the sum goes over all resonances $h_{*}$ which are the solutions of (64). The derivative of matrix $K_{G}^{\prime}(h)$ is

$$ \frac{1}{K_{G}^{\prime}(h)}=\frac{v_{h}w_{h}}{k_{G}^{\prime}(h)}\,, $$

where $v_{h}$ and $w_{h}$ are the corresponding right and left eigenvectors of $K_{G}(h)$ respectively which have eigenvalue $k_{G}(h)=1$ and normalized as $w_{h}v_{h}=1$ . Finally, we can rewrite (65) into the form

$$ \begin{split}\delta G(\tau)&=-\sum_{h=h_{*}}\alpha_{h}v_{h}\frac{G^{c}(\tau)}{|J\tau|^{h-1}}\,,\\
\alpha_{h}&=-\frac{w_{h}W_{\Sigma}(h)\vec{\sigma}_{h}}{k_{G}^{\prime}(h)}\,.\end{split} $$

We remark that the values of $\vec{\sigma}_{h}$ and thus $\alpha_{h}$ are not accessible in the IR because a physical UV source such as $\sigma(\tau)=(\partial_{\tau}-\mu)\delta(\tau)$ is highly singular and the task of decomposing it into asymptotic powerlaws perhaps is equivalent to solving the full Schwinger-Dyson equations. Below in the Section VII we present numerical results for $\alpha_{h}$ of the first few resonances in the bosonic and fermionic SYK4 models. The UV parameters $\alpha_{h}$ depend on the asymmetry angle $\theta$ and $q$ 22 2 We notice that $\alpha_{0}$ for $h_{0}=2$ resonance in the Majorana SYK model was computed numerically in Ref. [6] and denoted there as $\alpha_{G}$ . Moreover $\alpha_{G}$ was defined with respect to $\mathcal{J}=2^{(1-q)/2}\sqrt{q}J$ and therefore for $q=4$ we have $\alpha_{0}=\sqrt{2}\alpha_{G}$ . Below we present explicit formulas for the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the matrix $K_{G}(h)$ :

$$ \displaystyle k_{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}(h,\theta)=\frac{\Gamma(2\Delta-h)\Gamma(2\Delta+h-1)}{\Gamma(2\Delta+1)\Gamma(2\Delta-1)}\Bigg(2\Delta-1+\frac{\cos(2\theta)\sin(\pi h)}{\sin(2\pi\Delta)}\mp\sqrt{P}\Bigg)\,, \displaystyle v_{h}^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{1+(2\Delta-1)\frac{\sin(\pi h)}{\sin(2\pi\Delta)}}\begin{pmatrix}\frac{\sin(2\theta)}{\sin(2\pi\Delta)}(2\Delta-1-\cos(\pi h))\pm\sqrt{P}\\
1+\frac{\sin(2\theta)}{\sin(2\pi\Delta)}+(2\Delta-1)\frac{\sin(\pi h-2\theta)}{\sin(2\pi\Delta)}\end{pmatrix}\,, $$

where

$$ P=\sin(2\theta)^{2}\Bigl(1-\frac{\sin(\pi h)^{2}}{\sin(2\pi\Delta)^{2}}\Bigr)+\Bigl(\cos(2\theta)+(2\Delta-1)\frac{\sin(\pi h)}{\sin(2\pi\Delta)}\Bigr)^{2}\,. $$

Also $w_{h}^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}(\theta)$ can be expressed through $v_{h}^{\textrm{S}/\textrm{A}}(\theta)$ as $w_{h}^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}(\theta)=v_{h}^{\textrm{S}/\textrm{A}}(-\theta)^{\textrm{T}}\sigma_{z}/(v_{h}^{\textrm{S}/\textrm{A}}(-\theta)^{\textrm{T}}\sigma_{z}v_{h}^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}(\theta))$ , where $\sigma_{z}$ is the third Pauli matrix and one can check that $w_{h}^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}v_{h}^{\textrm{S}/\textrm{A}}=0$ . We notice that for $\theta=0$ the eigenvalues $k_{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}(h)$ in (68) coincide with definition (26). Though for non-zero asymmetry angle $\theta$ there is no symmetry under $\tau\to-\tau$ we still label eigenvalues and eigenvectors with $\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}$ indices. We denote by $h^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}$ solutions of the equations $k_{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}(h,\theta)=1$ and numerate them as $h^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}_{0},h^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}_{1},h^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}_{2},\dots$ . For these solutions we denote $\alpha_{h}$ as $\alpha_{0}^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}},\alpha_{1}^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}},\dots$ and similarly $v_{0}^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}},v_{1}^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}},\dots$ . In Fig.3 we plot $h^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}$ and corresponding $k^{\prime}_{{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}}}(h^{\textrm{A}/\textrm{S}})$ for the fermionic and bosonic SYK4 models as functions of the asymmetry angles $\theta_{f}$ and $\theta_{\mathfrak{b}}$ . We remark that in the fermionic model for $\theta_{f}=\pi/6$ some solutions of the equation $k_{\textrm{S}}(h)=1$ (red lines) go into solutions of $k_{\textrm{A}}(h)=1$ (blue lines), nevertheless we still denote the dimension of the whole line by $h^{\textrm{A}}$ . In bosonic case this happens for $\theta_{\mathfrak{b}}=\pi/3$ .
